utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I will now briefly outline the Trial Chamber's findings and sentence, the appeals, and how we will conduct the proceedings. The trial judgement was rendered on the 10th of June, 2010, by Trial Chamber II, composed of Judge Agius, Judge Kwon, and Judge Prost. The late Judge Ole Bjorn Stole was the Reserve Judge. The Trial Chamber found that a criminal enterprise existed to murder able-bodied Bosnian Muslim men from Srebrenica in July 1995 and that a joint criminal enterprise existed to forcibly remove the Bosnian Muslim population from Srebrenica and Zepa in 1995. With respect to Mr. Popovic and Mr. Beara, the Trial Chamber found them guilty of committing, as participants in the JCE to murder, genocide; conspiracy to commit genocide; extermination, as a crime against humanity; murder, as a crime against humanity and as a violation of the laws or customs of war; and persecution, as a crime against humanity. Mr. Popovic and Mr. Beara were both sentenced to life imprisonment. The Trial Chamber found Mr. Nikolic guilty of aiding and abetting genocide; and committing, as a participant in the JCE to murder, extermination, as a crime against humanity; murder, as a crime against humanity and as a violation of the laws or customs of war; and persecution, as a crime against humanity. Mr. Nikolic was sentenced to 35 years' imprisonment. The Trial Chamber found Mr. Miletic guilty, as a participant in the JCE to forcibly remove, of murder, as a crime against humanity, by majority, Judge Kwon dissenting; and persecution and inhumane acts, forcible transfer, as crimes against humanity. Mr. Miletic was sentenced to 19 years' imprisonment. With respect to Mr. Pandurevic, the Trial Chamber found him guilty of aiding and abetting murder, as a crime against humanity and as a violation of the laws or customs of war, by majority, with Judge Kwon dissenting; aiding and abetting persecution and inhumane acts, forcible transfer, as crimes against humanity; and murder, as a crime against humanity and as violation of the law or customs of war, pursuant to Article 7(3) of the Statute. Mr. Pandurevic was sentenced to 13 years' imprisonment. Following the rendering of the trial judgement, the Prosecution, Mr. Popovic, Mr. Beara, Mr. Nikolic, Mr. Miletic, and Mr. Pandurevic appealed the trial judgement. Let me now turn to the appeals. In its grounds of appeal, the Prosecution requests the Appeals Chamber to, inter alia, one, convict Mr. Pandurevic of committing extermination as a crime against humanity, murder as a violation of the laws or customs of war, and persecution as a crime against humanity through his membership in the JCE to murder, or, alternatively, for aiding and abetting extermination as a crime against humanity, murder as a violation of the laws or customs of war, and persecution as a crime against humanity of Bosnian Muslim civilians; two, convict Mr. Pandurevic for having failed to prevent and punish his subordinates for their criminal acts; and, three, revise Mr. Pandurevic's sentence. In their responses, Mr. Pandurevic, Mr. Popovic, Mr. Nikolic, and Mr. Miletic oppose the Prosecution's appeal as far as they are individually concerned, while Mr. Beara did not respond. Mr. Popovic's appeal brief did not follow the order of the grounds set out in his Notice of Appeal. Rather, he raises contentions under ten different titles, requesting the Appeals Chamber to reverse the convictions entered by the Trial Chamber and to enter a verdict of not guilty on all counts. Alternatively, he requests the Appeals Chamber to quash all convictions and to order a new trial or to reduce his sentence. The Prosecution submits that the Appeals Chamber should dismiss Mr. Popovic's appeal in its entirety. Mr. Beara submits 40 grounds of appeal, requesting the Appeals Chamber to grant him a new trial, to dismiss the charges or to substantially reduce the sentence imposed on him. In response, the Prosecution submits that Mr. Beara's appeal should be dismissed in its entirety. Mr. Nikolic advances 22 grounds of appeal. He requests that the Appeals Chamber quash his convictions. Alternatively, he requests a revision of sentence, and depending on which grounds of appeal are granted, he proposes what the new sentence should be. The Prosecution responds that Mr. Nikolic's appeal should be dismissed in its entirety. Mr. Miletic presents 28 grounds of appeal, requesting that either the trial judgement be quashed and his case be remanded to the Trial Chamber for a trial de novo or that his sentence be reduced. He further submits that the Appeals Chamber should rescind the confidentiality of the trial judgement which was rendered both in a confidential and publicly redacted version. The Prosecution responds that Mr. Miletic's ground of appeal should be dismissed with the exception of ground of appeal 6 with respect to forcible transfer as a crime against humanity. Mr. Pandurevic presents four grounds of appeal, requesting the Appeals Chamber to quash all his convictions and either, in addition or in the alternative, to reduce his sentence. In response, the Prosecution requests that the Appeals Chamber dismiss Mr. Pandurevic's appeal in its entirety. I bring to your attention the timetable set out in the order for the agenda of the appeal hearing issued on 7th November 2013. I encourage the parties to use their allotted time wisely, bearing in mind the questions that the Appeals Chamber raised in the order for the preparation of the appeal hearing of 6 November 2013. It has been well said that brevity is the soul of wit. I say brevity is also the soul of good lawyering. I now invite counsel for Mr. Popovic to present his submissions. I just make one other comment on housekeeping. It's that although the breaks have been set at 15 minutes, evidently we were being overzealous, and we have been asked by the technical people that the break be 20 minutes. So the breaks will be 20 minutes. Counsel for Mr. Popovic, you may present your submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. In presenting Popovic appeal today, I will argue that the Trial Chamber made factual errors resulting in a miscarriage of justice. These errors concern the joint criminal enterprise which allegedly emerged before and in the morning on 12 July 1995 and Popovic's participation therein.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. I neglected to say that you have 75 minutes. Of course, nothing obliges you to use all of that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will then describe the subsequent errors related to the conviction of Mr. Popovic for genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes, committed after the fall of Srebrenica in July 1995, and Popovic's alleged genocidal intent. I shall also show that the Trial Chamber's assessment of crucial evidence departed from the standards for a reasonable trier of fact and that of beyond a reasonable doubt. Such evidence includes that of PW101, 168, Srecko Acimovic, and Momir Nikolic, as well as some documents. I will then turn the floor over to Ms. Tapuskovic and she will respond to the questions put by Your Honours. And she will argue that factual errors were made in respect of the numbers of victims including the murders allegedly committed on 13 July 1995 at Jadar River, Rasica Gaj and Cerska Valley, as described in our brief in paragraphs 203 through 210. I will first demonstrate how the Trial Chamber's assessment of the evidence was unreasonable. Paragraphs 8 through 16 of Popovic's brief referred the jurisprudence establishing the standards of reasonable Trial Chamber, and the standard beyond a reasonable doubt. I will not repeat it in my oral submission. As discussed in the brief, Momir Nikolic was the Trial Chamber's sole source that the plan to murder Bosnian Muslim men in Potocari began before the third Hotel Fontana meeting at 10.00 on 12 July 1995. This was in error. On the basis of Momir Nikolic's evidence, the Trial Chamber found that Popovic had genocidal intent due to his knowledge of the plan to murder from the time of its inception. I refer to trial judgement paragraph 1178. Resting on his testimony about discussion in Bratunac before the operation began and statement that all balijas have to be killed. It's in paragraph 1179 of the trial judgement. I'll not repeat our arguments set out in paragraphs 34 through 168 of the brief except to state that the Trial Chamber selectively read the transcript as demonstrated in paragraphs 40 to 46 of the brief, that the Chamber erroneously relied on the errors in Nikolic's statement of facts, as described in paragraphs 47 to 49 of the brief, while disregarding the flagrant inconsistencies between the statement of facts and Nikolic's testimony, as described in paragraphs 50 to 64 of the brief. The Chamber also completely disregarded a bulk of evidence which proves that the separation process dealt solely with the screening, as described in paragraphs 65 through 73. Paragraph 66, footnote 107, of Popovic's brief referred to evidence provided by Prosecution witnesses, Muslim prisoners, DutchBat officers, and officers of the Army of Republika Srpska who testified about the screening carried out on 12 and 13 July 1995. The list of war criminals dated on 12 July 1995 strongly demonstrated that the main objective of the separation in Potocari was to identify potential war criminals. Indeed, as a result of these screenings, many Muslim men left Potocari to the Muslim-held territory, as described in paragraphs 157 through 162 of the brief. The screening efforts actually demonstrated the intent of the Bosnian Serb forces to identify war crime suspects. The screening process disproves that the plan to kill Muslim men in Potocari was the only reasonable conclusion from the evidence. Popovic also indicated that the prisoners from Potocari were in the purview of civilian authorities from 11 until 14 July 1995. Exhibit P10 proved that the citizens from Srebrenica who participated in combat against Army of Republika Srpska were under jurisdiction of the newly appointed commissioner for Srebrenica, Miroslav Deronjic, as described in paragraph 81 of the brief. The DutchBat officer Boering discussed the evacuation and separation issues after the third Hotel Fontana meeting with the representatives of the civilian authorities, as described in paragraph 80 and 83 of the brief. Prosecution Witness 162's activities demonstrated that the civilian authorities had jurisdiction over Srebrenica civilians. This includes Mladic's introduction of Deronjic to international service as such, as described in paragraph 84 and 85 of the brief. Finally, Beara's conversation with Deronjic on the night of 13 July as recounted by the Trial Chamber at paragraph 1264 of the judgement strongly indicated that, at that time, the civilian authorities were responsible for the prisoners, as described in paragraphs 86 through 88 of the brief. Therefore, a discussion, alleged discussion, between Popovic, Momir Nikolic and Kosoric on the accommodation of prisoners in sites in and around Bratunac, among them as military officers, would have been outside the jurisdiction, outside their scope of responsibility and therefore unfeasible, as described in paragraphs 74 through 88 of the brief. The brief established and the Trial Chamber neglected to acknowledge that Momir Nikolic had every incentive to incriminate himself for ordering of the execution of prisoners at Kravica warehouse and Sandici, as described in paragraphs 89 through 99 of the brief. The Trial Chamber overlooked that, in the course of plea agreement negotiations, his purported confessions to such a terrible crime was at first rejected by the Prosecution, prompting him to then falsely incriminate others, including Popovic. Knowing that the Prosecution was looking for the plan to murder, Nikolic invented the conversation with Popovic and Kosoric on 12 July in front of the Hotel Fontana. In the end, that was the only piece of evidence about the plan to kill Muslim men emerging before 10.00 in the morning on 12 July 1995. The Chamber erroneously concluded that Nikolic diminished his role and the responsibility in Potocari. However, Popovic asserts that the parts of his statement concerning his coordinating role is false; namely, only commanders of the units could have a coordinating role in the command and control of various military units. Nikolic was not a commander of any unit and could not coordinate activities of various units in Potocari. As a non-commissioned officer, his military knowledge was very limited. His statement of facts and subsequent testimonies showed a lack of military -- of familiarity with key military terms. For instance, his discussion of the coordination of various units neglected that a coordinator holds command authority and issue orders, a fact that he would deny to evade responsibility if he knew its true meaning. It is described in paragraphs 115 to 118 of the brief. The Trial Chamber was beguiled by Nikolic, arguing that his demeanour was credible on certain issues but not others. The Chamber did not explain how Nikolic's demeanour during untruthful part of his testimony differed from when he allegedly testified truthfully. It is addressed in paragraphs 119 through 121 of the brief. In any event, the finding disregarded the obvious contradictions in his evidence. The Chamber's attempt to provide evidence to corroborate Nikolic's testimony fell short. This is in -- these are paragraphs 284 through 288 of the judgement, and it was addressed in the brief in paragraphs 122 through 126. The Trial Chamber's finding of a plan to commit genocide centred on the content of the purported conversation between Popovic, Nikolic and others in front of the Hotel Fontana on 12 July. However, nothing in the evidence used by the Trial Chamber corroborates Nikolic's testimony in any way, supported the content of the discussion, if any, that the men had to be killed at the time. Meanwhile, the testimony of Defence Witness Kosoric, who denied the conversation described by Nikolic in front of the Fontana Hotel, was conveniently dismissed. It was analysed in paragraphs 127 to 157 of the brief. The Trial Chamber also erred in finding that the plan to murder expanded to include the captured men in the -- from the column. Though the Trial Chamber found, for instance, that heavy combat operations were ongoing on 12 and 13 July - for example in the paragraphs 365, 371, 376 of the judgement - the Trial Chamber nevertheless construed that Mladic's order gagging all discussion of military activities was evidence of a murder plan. The order restricted movements for uninvited persons in Srebrenica and Zepa regions and closed roads leading to the battlefields. The order instructed brigade commanders to ban and prevent the release of information to media regarding combat activities, prisoners of war, evacuated civilians, escapees. These restrictions obviously served to prevent Muslim forces from becoming aware of the army's movement and plans. A further list of contradictions and inconsistencies as to this misconstruction may be found in paragraphs 171 through 178 of Popovic's brief. The Chamber also erred in relying on other evidence in order to find that Popovic issued an order to Jokic not to mention prisoners in written and radio communication and that that order was sent through the line of command on 13 July. Popovic would not have issued such instruction to Jokic; namely, Jokic was, as chief of the security -- namely, Jokic was the chief of engineering of the Zvornik Brigade. Popovic would send such instruction to the commandant of the Zvornik Brigade. Jokic was subordinate to Obrenovic at the time, who was the Chief of Staff and acting commander of the Zvornik Brigade. As the chief of engineering, Jokic could not issue the orders to the brigade. If Popovic had wanted to give or convey any order, he would not have issued to Jokic but to Obrenovic, who was the commander of the brigade at the time. It was addressed in our brief in paragraphs 179 through 180. Popovic also listed the evidence indicating that the plan to murder did not exist before 14 July 1995. It is in paragraphs 181 through 202 of the brief. The errors demonstrated in that part of the brief affects judgement's finding related to the expansion of the plan to murder to the men from the column on 13 July, as mentioned in paragraphs 857, 858, and 861 of the judgement. Popovic's brief showed why the killings in the Kravica warehouse and Sandici meadow were not a part of the plan to murder. They need to be repeated today, but -- they need not be repeated today, but I invite Your Honours to review paragraphs 211 through 214 of the brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: (redacted), it's in paragraphs 223 --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I refer Your Honours to the jurisprudence on plea agreement witnesses from Judge Prisca Matimba Nyambe's dissenting and separate concurring opinions in the judgement in Tolimir. This is in paragraph 5 to 13 of that judgement. The witnesses invented intermediaries to convince the Prosecution to accept their pleas and diverted attention away from their own culpability, as described in paragraphs 233 through 237. For all due caution, I would move to the private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The significant contradictions in the evidence of the plea agreement witnesses set out in paragraph --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honours, we are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. The significant contradictions in the evidence of the plea agreement witnesses set out in paragraphs 238 to 268 just confirm their lies. These factual errors impact the Trial Chamber's findings that Popovic knew about the plan to murder. The Chamber furthermore erred by finding Popovic direct participation in the murders in Grbavci school, Rocevic, and Pilica. It is in paragraph 269 of the brief. Contrary to the Trial Chamber's finding, Popovic was not present at the two execution sites: Lazete 1, also known as Orahovac, in the evening of 14 July, and Branjevo on 16 July. No witness identified Popovic at any execution site. PW-101 described a Lieutenant Colonel or Colonel from the Drina Corps at the execution site in Lazete 1 but did not know his name. He also did not identify him. Instead, the Trial Chamber used circumstantial evidence to find that this officer was Popovic. It was analysed in paragraphs 285 through 298 of our brief. The testimony of PW-101 is in any event untrue, as described in paragraph 299 through 308. In particular, Popovic extensively named other evidence which contradicts the testimony of PW-101 as demonstrated in paragraph 301. The credibility of this witness has been obviously demonstrated after the judgement when he retracted highly relevant parts of his testimony, denying even that he said --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry to rise at this point. This is the -- this is subject to an outstanding Rule 115 application which has not been ruled upon. This material is not in the record and should not be submitted upon at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That would seem to be correct. Counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. I agree. I'll omit it from my submission. Thank you. While his commander testified that PW-101 was sent to Orahovac in order to pick up Sreten Milosevic, deputy commander for logistics in the Zvornik Brigade, as described in paragraph 301(a), PW-101 inexplicably recalled being sent there to drop off provisions. He also concealed from the Chamber that he himself never went to the execution site while the executions were taking place. According to Witness 3DW10, PW-101 never saved young boy from the execution site, as described in paragraph 301(c) and (d). Rather, he picked him up in front of the school nearby. PW-101 misrepresented that only he was with the boy in the van during the drive to Zvornik, as described in 301(e), and that he drove the van straight from the execution site to the Zvornik hospital, as described in paragraph 301(f). But other witnesses clearly recalled accompanying him. Finally, he lied that he was present at the execution site Lazete 1 on the evening of 14 July. These executions took place in the night after the executions at Lazete 2 had been completed. PW-110, a survivor of the execution, attested to this. The account of the event from these various witnesses is too inconsistent to prove to a reasonable Chamber, beyond a reasonable doubt, that Popovic was present in Orahovac on 14 July. It was addressed in paragraphs 305 to 307 of the appeal brief. The Trial Chamber's credibility assessment of PW-101 is unsustainable as he's the subject of a pending Rule 115 motion. Therefore, the Trial Chamber's finding that the officer present at Lazete 1 while the execution was taking place is not the only reasonable conclusion from the evidence. The Chamber made a more drastic error by finding that the officer who was described by Drazen Erdemovic was Popovic. Erdemovic described the officer as a very corpulent man with no mustaches or beard. Popovic is 174 centimetres and had mustache at the time. Erdemovic did not recognise Popovic in the photo lineup. The Trial Chamber nevertheless concluded that this officer was Popovic. It was addressed in our brief in paragraphs 271 through 282. The Trial Chamber used -- the Trial Chamber's use of the fuel request to bolster its findings about Branjevo erred in three ways. First, the Chamber failed to acknowledge that Popovic did not necessarily make the request personally. As assistant commander of the Drina Corps, Popovic would need to request the fuel directly from his command. He would not make such a request through the Zvornik Brigade. If he could contact the Zvornik Brigade, he was also able to communicate with the Drina Corps command. Second, meanwhile, timing of both the request and its delivery did not effectively coincide such that it would in any way assist the executions. Finally, a request for fuel is at odds with other documents which concretely demonstrate that the machines used for burials were filled at the gas station in Zvornik. This topic and others have been additionally undermined by evidence which we have submitted in Rule 115 motion. This finding is not the only reasonable conclusion from the evidence. Also, the Trial Chamber erred by finding that the intercept of 17 July 1995 was related to the killing and burials of the Muslim prisoners. It is addressed in paragraph 341. In its interpretation, the Chamber disregarded dots in the text which clearly indicated missing words in the conversation, as described in paragraph 343 through 345. In addition, the Trial Chamber disregarded that Popovic received an order to visit Baljkovica in the afternoon of 16 July to deal with the opening of the corridor, as described in paragraphs 346 to 350 of the brief. According to the Defence Witness Rakic, the corridor was a highly urgent and important issue at the time. Indeed, even three high-ranking officers from the Main Staff were sent to double-check the reports about the corridor submitted by Pandurevic and later Popovic. I will next show how the Chamber also erred in finding that Popovic had a coordinating role in Orahovac, Rocevic, and Branjevo. It's paragraphs 283 through 284. The role of Popovic, his alleged presence, acts and conduct in Rocevici on 15 July in the morning is analysed in paragraphs 309 to 335 of Popovic's brief. According to the Trial Chamber, Popovic arrived in front of the Rocevic school to kill prisoners, without men, ammunition, trucks, or even a possible location to carry it out. The three Prosecution witnesses who were present in front of Rocevic school - it is in paragraph 318 of our brief - in no way confirmed Acimovic's testimony. It is addressed in paragraphs 326 and 331 to 335 of the brief. The Chamber did not clearly assess the testimony of two of them, as described in paragraph 320, and distorted the evidence of one, as described in paragraph 321 through 322. For corroboration, the Trial Chamber illogically confused correlation with causation. The Chamber could only find proof of Acimovic's account by looking at the subsequent acts of Acimovic and others. This is not evidence of Popovic's accountability. Moreover, their evidence as well as documents adduced strongly indicated that Acimovic himself organised the provision of ammunition, vehicles and men for execution of prisoners in Rocevici and determined Kozluk as the execution site. However, he concealed the actual superior or superiors who ordered him to do that as explained in paragraphs 317 and 326. Finally, the Trial Chamber failed to acknowledge the testimony of Prosecution Witness Dragan Todorovic who saw Popovic in Dragasevac at the time when he was allegedly in Rocevic. It is transcript pages 14026. I will now discuss how the Trial Chamber made errors as to Popovic's custody of the ten wounded prisoners from the Standard barracks. It is in the brief in paragraphs 357 through 360. The Chamber misconstrued the content of two intercepts, as described in Popovic's brief in paragraphs 361 through 365, and vehicle logbook for his Golf, as described in paragraph 366 to 367. Moreover, the Chamber disregarded

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Chamber found, inter alia, that Popovic's Golf car travelled to Zvornik but did not resolve whether Popovic travelled in that car on that day. The Chamber was also ambiguous about the stay of the Milic patients in the Zvornik hospital before they transferred to the Zvornik Brigade, as described in paragraph 369. The Trial Chamber disregarded the evidence of Dr. Novakovic, who brought the wounded Muslims from Milici in the late afternoon on 14 July but did not find them in the hospital in the morning of 15 July, as described in paragraph 370 of the brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
