utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think we should stay in the private session, Your Honours. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: As a matter of caution, okay, yes, we will stay in private session but tell us when we will exit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber also disregarded the testimony of Dr. Zoran Begovic who confirmed that all instructions as to these patients he had received from Obrenovic who made all arrangements about their transfer, accommodation, and medical treatment by the personnel from the Zvornik hospital. He even instructed Dr. Begovic not to register these patients into the register book of the Zvornik Brigade infirmary. It is in paragraphs 371 through 373 of the brief; transcript pages 9137 through 9138 and 9140. The evidence also indicated that the securing of the Zvornik medical centre arose on 14 July 1995, the same day when the wounded Muslims were transferred from Milici. That task was carried out by Obrenovic's subordinate, Mihajlo Galic, who would have done so only on Obrenovic's order. It's paragraph 374. The information about the death of one of the wounded Muslims in the Zvornik hospital, sent in the early morning hours of 16 July, strongly demonstrated that the other wounded Muslims had been already transferred to the Zvornik Brigade by that date and not on the 20th, as the Trial Chamber held. It is described in our brief in paragraphs 377 and 378. One of the missing patients was treated in the morning on 14 July 1995 by Dr. Novakovic and sent to the Standard barracks - it is in paragraph 379 of our brief - showing that these patients were sent to Zvornik Brigade infirmary on 14 July. All these facts indicate that it was not only reasonable conclusion from the evidence that Popovic killed or facilitated killing of the wounded Muslim patients. The next issue that I shall challenge involves Bisina. These events were not the part of the indictment, as described in paragraphs 387 through 401. The Chamber disregarded the evidence presented by the Defence, indicating that in the morning of 23 July, when the events in Bisina took place, Popovic went to Zvornik where he met the manager of the Vezionica factory, Vlacic. Although Vlacic could not remember the exact date of the meeting but distinctly recalled that he asked about Popovic's relative, Djordje Popovic, who was wounded and captured in the action near Zepa. At 9.00 in the morning of 23 July, the duty officer of the Drina Corps, Jevitski reported to the Drina Corps commander, General Krstic, that Popovic went to Vlacic. It is in paragraph 395. The vehicle logbook for the Golf used by Popovic also registered his travel from Vlasenica to Zvornik and back, as described in paragraph 396. Two other witnesses who worked on the construction of the barracks in Bisina described that Popovic arrived there two or three hours after the trucks and showed him the road. Popovic went there and came back shortly thereafter. Cumulatively, these evidence confirm that Popovic arrived at Bisina after the execution of the prisoners. Popovic challenged the finding of the Chamber that Bosnian Serb forces committed genocide, as described in paragraphs 19 through 32 of the brief. According to the Chamber's definition, Bosnian Serb forces include many thousands of members, the majority which had not any role in the events in Srebrenica. The judgement did not identify any specific member of the Bosnian Serb forces that possessed genocidal intent except Popovic and Beara. Judicial fairness requires that the genocidal intent of the perpetrator must be established only on a case-by-case basis. For example, the perpetrator of the execution of Muslim prisoners at Branjevo military farm, Drazen Erdemovic, was not convicted for genocide, as he lacked genocidal intent. So far, the ICTY tried 11 accused for the Srebrenica mass killings. None -- none of the units' commanders from the Drina Corps were found guilty for genocide, for the lack of genocidal intent. Yet, according to the Trial Chamber, untold and unknown members of the Bosnian Serb forces nevertheless possessed such intent. The finding that members of the Bosnian Serb forces committed genocide violates the presumption of innocence and introduced instead the presumption of guilt of genocide for any members of the Bosnian Serb forces. It is notable, however, that such a finding was necessary pillar for finding Popovic's genocidal intent. Without such finding, the genocidal intent would be restricted to just two medium-ranking VRS officers, Popovic and Beara. The acts of the Bosnian Serb forces at the time demonstrated that they transported between 20- and 30.000 Muslims to the safety of the Muslim-held territory. In addition, despite their awareness of the movement of the Muslim military column breaking through the Serb-held territory, the VRS sent its main forces in opposite direction, to Zepa. These acts clearly demonstrated the lack of genocidal intent on the part of the Bosnian Serb forces. The Chamber took two elements as the proof of genocidal intent, a significant coordination, as described in trial judgement -- in paragraphs 882 and 933, and the vast process. It is Popovic's submission that neither significant coordination nor a vast process are distinctive elements of genocide. Indeed, war crimes or crimes against humanity, if not all crimes with more than two co-perpetrators, may process the same characteristics, as described by the Trial Chamber. Popovic analysed in details these errors in paragraphs 19 to 32 of his brief. I now give the floor to Mrs. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to the colleagues from the Prosecution. One part of the appeal brief for Vujadin Popovic relates to the victims of Srebrenica, to the persons gone missing, executed, identified. And in that appeal, we submit that the Trial Chamber erred in establishing the total number of missing, in establishing the total number of deceased, in including the total -- among those killed the victims from Nova Kasaba, and including in the total number of killed the victims that were at locations not alleged in the indictment, and in going beyond the scope of the indictment in establishing, among those killed, some who were not alleged in the indictment. We would like to refer you right now to 607 paragraph from Trial Chamber where it is stated that the precise number of deceased is not necessary in order to reach a conclusion regarding the crimes alleged in the indictment. And there we refer you to footnote 2214, a conclusion as to the number of persons killed does not form an element of the crimes alleged. However, the Trial Chamber also went on to say in the same paragraph that, however, such an estimate is relevant, particularly to the crime of genocide and extermination, a crime against humanity. Now, and in paragraphs 457 and 461 of our appeal brief, we asserted that the Trial Chamber erred in paragraph 659 and 664 by including among the persons missing the identities of persons that could not be matched with a single person from the list of missing, as well as the persons exchanged in Batkovic, who were later found to be alive. The Trial Chamber erred also by including in the total number of identified those persons who were not identified by their first or last name but only by their unique DNA profile. According to Janc, without identification one could not be sure that the remains belonged to individuals associated with the events following the fall of Srebrenica. This is something that the Trial Chamber itself found at paragraph 651 of the judgement. Consequently, the number of those identified should be reduced by the number of those who could not be matched with the list of missing, but in respect of whom we only have their unique DNA profile. At paragraph 441 of our appeal, we found that the Trial Chamber erred by adding to the number of persons executed also the surface remains found at the Kozluk site; whereas elsewhere in the judgement, at paragraphs 651, 659 and 660, other surface remains were excluded from the total number of victims. Therefore, we believe that a consistent approach should be adopted and the same approach should be adopted to these Kozluk surface remains. The Nova Kasaba victims were addressed in paragraphs 415 and 418 of the appeal brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Can you just clarify "surface remains"? What is meant by "the surface remains"?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The judgement extensively addressed the issue of surface remains. In the report by expert Janc, which is P4490, it was stated --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Ms. Tapuskovic please repeat the number of the victims she referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The interpreter is asking to you repeat the number of victims that you just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was stated that there was 648 sets of surface remains. May I proceed, Your Honour? Paragraph 30.3.1 of the indictment alleges the events at Nova Kasaba. However, the victims from Nova Kasaba, as the Trial Chamber itself found at footnote 6069, as alleged in the indictment, were not proven. In our view, therefore, that the total of 90 victims that were alleged to have been killed at Nova Kasaba should be deducted from the total number of victims established in paragraph 664 of the judgement because they were not proven to have been the victims of executions. This applies to all of the four graves of Nova Kasaba, 1996, 1999, 2001 and the individual grave. This is to be found in the Prosecution exhibit P4490, annex A, page 34 -- pages 3 and 4. This reduction should be carried out according to the same principle that was applied in paragraph 657, 661, 662, and 664 of the judgement, where the Trial Chamber reduced the total number of victims by 12 sets of mortal remains from the Glogova 1 grave, those were bodies that were brought back from Serbia, and by ten persons from the Cancari Road 4 grave. As stated by my colleague, Mr. Zivanovic, this was not alleged in the indictment, the location of Bisina was not alleged in the indictment and was only raised by the OTP as proof of the pattern of conduct of the accused Popovic, of his participation in the murder operation, and this is P4490, page 4, annex A, page 28. We believe that an error was made in this way, when arriving at the number -- at the total number of victims because these victims were not alleged in the indictment and were not part of the Prosecution case. In our appeal brief, paragraphs 460 and 463, those victims addressed in other graves were dealt with, and according to Janc, these were surface remains. This is P4490. In our submission, these persons who were identified there should be treated the same as other surface remains, as indicated in paragraph 651, 659 and 660, including 648. We also have persons exhumed among them who were from unknown locations, and since there was no information of their cause or place of death, Janc himself believed that they were to be treated as surface remains. Now, the Defence appeal brief at paragraph 6 -- 465 deals with the victims whose remains were recovered in Serbia. There is no proof of cause of death and therefore there is no proof of them being victims of murder. This is P4490, annex A, page 35. In our view, therefore, they should not be included among the total number of victims. Here we have to point out that the Trial Chamber in Tolimir arrived at entirely different conclusions and findings in their judgement, which were not appealed by the Prosecution. We are aware of the fact that the Trial Chamber in Tolimir used its discretion to establish certain facts. However, it is the -- a mission of this Tribunal to establish facts. It will be part of its legacy. And the mission includes, among other things, the practice for the Trial Chambers to rely upon the factual findings from other cases through adjudicated facts. We believe that the interests of justice would make such a conclusion imperative in this case as well. In the Tolimir trial judgement, at paragraphs 546 and 569, the Trial Chamber found that approximately 39 men were mentioned and alleged in the indictment in respect of Bisina, although the Trial Chamber itself found that 54 persons were killed. Although the number is bigger than the one alleged in the indictment, nevertheless, it goes beyond the scope of the indictment and the specific paragraph and therefore is not part of the case against the accused. As for the victims falling into the category of other graves, they are mentioned in the Trial Chamber against Popovic, just as they were in the Tolimir trial judgement. Now, the Tolimir Trial Chamber found at paragraph 590 that the forces of the Bosnian Serbs did not kill the victims mentioned in this category as victims hors de combat with the exception of the victims of Trnovo. In our case, unlike the Tolimir Trial Chamber, these victims were included in the total number of victims. Now, in the Tolimir judgement, the Kozluk surface remains were included in the category of other graves but were not included among the total number of victims. The Trial Chamber in our case did so. As for persons identified in other graves and those identified in Serbia, we can say the same thing that we said about Bisina; namely that these locations were not included in the indictment. We did not have any proof that this had to do with executions that were the result of the execution of a joint criminal enterprise to murder and their number should not be included in the overall number of victims. The indictment only refers to locations sites referred to in paragraphs 30.1 to 31.4, and other locations are not mentioned. The possibility that the killings occurred at other sites as well was not referred to by the Prosecution in their pre-trial brief, paragraphs 47 through 130, and not in their opening arguments, and that is an acceptable way to additionally clarify the indictment. That is part of the jurisprudence of this Tribunal as stated in the Naletilic judgement, paragraph 34. Your Honours, now we would like to deal with the questions that you put to the Popovic Defence. The questions were put along the following lines, I'm going to read out that in the English language now: [In English] To discuss Popovic submission that the Trial Chamber erred in convicting him for execution of more than thousand males at Kozluk on 15 July 1995, while the indictment only charged him with killing about 500 Muslim men at that location. [Interpretation] The first question of the Appeals Chamber was how the Trial Chamber interpreted 30.10 and 30.8.1 in the indictment in footnote 1839 of the trial judgement. In paragraph 30.8.1 of the indictment, it is stated that approximately 500 Bosnian Muslims, on the 14th or 15th of July, were detained at the school in Rocevici. In paragraph 30.10 of the indictment, it is stated that on the 15th of July, 1995, members of the Army of Republika Srpska and/or the MUP of the Republika Srpska transported about 500 Bosnian Muslims to a location near Kozluk and executed them summarily, and on the following day they were buried. That paragraph, 30.10 of the indictment, does not state where the Bosnian Muslims had been brought from. By reading the indictment itself, the school in Rocevici cannot easily be linked to Kozluk. However, the body of evidence that was adduced during the trial, in terms of what happened at the school in Rocevici and in Kozluk, unequivocally shows that the detainees from the school in Rocevici were transported to Kozluk. The judgement, in paragraph 516, states that the prisoners from the school in Rocevici were transported to Kozluk together with the corpses that had already been seen in front of the school, and that is confirmed in footnote 1839. The position of the Defence is that footnote 1839 of the judgement is very clear. It is on page 199 of the judgement and the title is: "The school in Rocevici and Kozluk." We wish to note on this occasion that the prisoners from the school in Rocevici were killed in Kozluk and these were the persons involved in one single transaction as is defined in Rule 2 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. We believe that the judgement, in terms of paragraph 516 and footnote 1839, corrected a shortcoming of the indictment that did not properly link the Rocevici school and Kozluk. As regards the second question that was put by the Appeals Chamber to the Popovic Defence, and it reads as follows: [In English] Whether Popovic was convicted for any killings in excess of those pleaded in these two provisions. [Interpretation] In paragraph 524 of the judgement, the Trial Chamber asserts that 1040 persons identified and linked to Kozluk primary and secondary graves, seven of them on the road to Cancari 2, 3, 4, 5 in particular, 7, and 13. The Defence believes that one of the basic principles of criminal procedure is that one should not go beyond the scope of the indictment. We believe that a Court cannot find someone responsible for anything that goes beyond the allegations made in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Counsel, just to observe that there is just about three or four minutes before the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that I will manage to finish within those three or four minutes, and thank you for having said that. May I continue? Thank you. Changing the number of victims is not a substantive change. That is not a material fact in legal terms. It does not mean adding new crimes in addition to the existing ones. All the elements of the crimes that have been charged would remain the same. It is just a question as to whether this number is part of the Prosecution case against the accused. Whether there were 500 victims at one location or 1.000 victims is a question of fact, not a legal question, but it is a legal question whether somebody is -- whether somebody can be found guilty for over 1.000 victims and the indictment charges about 500. In the judgement, in paragraph 523, Cancarski Put number 5 where 283 persons were identified, P4490, paragraph -- annex A, pages 11 and 37, the judgement links this to Kozluk because Janc also links it to Kozluk. However, the Janc report, in the Tolimir case, links this grave to Branjevo, a completely different location.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry to rise. It's really not appropriate to refer to evidence in another case in this case when there is no evidence on the record. If my learned friend wished to make applications to bring that evidence into the record, Rule 115 is the correct route to do so. And whilst I'm on my feet, there have been a number of references to the Tolimir trial judgement. That also is not appropriate, to make references to another judgement dealing with the same issues or some of the same issues because, of course, the evidential record in that case is different to the evidential record in this case. So my learned friend should not make references to the other judgements that may deal with these issues because they are not within the four square walls of this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will take the break now, counsel. 20 minutes. --- Break taken at 11.30 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Rogers, I find that while there are elements of correctness in your last submission, overall I conclude it's not correct, it's not correct to say counsel can't refer to the -- to another case. The cases are public document. Of course, it will be a matter for the Appeals Chamber to determine what weight to attach, what value to attach to the reference. In this particular instance, I note that the Tolimir case is on appeal and the Appeals Chamber would, of course, take that into account in assessing the value of the reference. In other instances, we have the rule that factual findings by a Chamber in one case are not binding on another Chamber. So in all the circumstances, I believe that your submission, your objection, was a little extreme. Counsel may make the reference and the Chamber will determine the value to attach to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I make a brief comment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, my concern is this, that if evidence from another case is being referred to, as my learned friend did in relation to a report by a particular witness, that evidence should be on the record in this case, and the route to do that is through Rule 115. Otherwise, the Court will be taking into account considerations based upon evidence that is not on the record in this case. Likewise, if there are findings of fact from another case, then the correct route would be an adjudicated facts motion but I simply can't see how that could possibly occur in proceedings on appeal. The problem with an appeal is that is ring-fenced by the evidence within the record and any other material outside of the evidence on the record is simply not admissible unless the Appeals Chamber has determined that it should come in in an admissible form, and it has not. And so there are no circumstances in which, on appeal, the Appeals Chamber can take notice of factual or other findings in other cases, in my submission, to inform you as to the arguments that are being made on the evidence on the record in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I still find it a little extreme. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Your decision was made before I wanted to add just one sentence. I thought that the Prosecution should have waited for me to finish the sentence that I had started because I was not invoking any evidence from Tolimir. I just wanted to invoke paragraphs 480, 481, 581, with footnote 2564, and paragraph 596 of the Tolimir judgement. As for Cancarski Put number 5, it links it to Branjevo not to Kozluk anymore. Because of the role of this Tribunal and because of the need for historical facts to be recorded properly, we need to take that into account as well. I shall proceed now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before you continue, just one housekeeping matter has been brought to my attention. It's that if a particular party concludes his or her submissions before the time allotted, then the other party should be ready to take up the slack. Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 480, 481, 486, 591, link only 761 persons to Kozluk. If we were to subtract grave Cancari Road 5, because it was established that it was related to Cancari, we would have a number less than 1.000 victims related to Kozluk. The Kozluk primary and secondary graves, that is. The position of the Defence is that the number of over 1.000 Muslims killed in Kozluk goes beyond what is stated in paragraphs 30.8.1 and 30.10 of the indictment and was not part of the Prosecution case against the accused. I think that in this way I responded to both of the questions put by the Trial Chamber, and now I would like to go on for another two minutes, speaking about the other matters related to the Popovic appeal. In paragraphs 432 to 436 as regards Orahovac, the Defence would like to say that in the case of Orahovac and the number of victims of the execution at that location, the situation is the same as with Kozluk, namely that one went beyond the indictment. As for Orahovac, the indictment, in paragraph 30.6, says that on the 13th and 14th of July, 1995, hundreds of Bosnian Muslims were transported to the school in Grbavci, and that on the 14th of July, they were transported to a nearby meadow where approximately 1.000 Bosnian Muslims were executed. In paragraph 1788, along with paragraph 492, the Trial Chamber states that several witnesses testified about Grbavci, a total of four of them, and they gave an approximation, approximate range, of 1.000 to 2.500 persons who were detained in the school. In the judgement, no elements were provided to establish beyond a reasonable doubt that the number of executed persons at that location could have exceeded the number of 2.500. We believe that one went beyond the indictment there as well because the number of 2.500 victims goes beyond the assertions made in paragraph 30.6 of the indictment and were not part of the Prosecution case against the accused. In paragraphs 455, 472 through 474 of the appeal, there was a reference to the Janc report. The Defence states that excessive importance was attached to it because it does not meet the standards required of an expert report. We have already pointed out the differences in his summaries and the findings in the Tolimir case, and in this case, that are based on his updated summaries, lead us to conclude that his summary is unreliable and most importantly contradictory. As regards all the other things stated in the appeal, with regard to missing persons, victims, and other matters, we stand by what we said in the appeal brief that will not be elaborated upon today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Rogers?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm conscious of the scheduling order and the time set out in the scheduling order, and I see we -- although just having had a break, we've come to the time allotted for Your Honours' lunchtime break. Does Your Honour wish me to continue for five minutes, or are you and your colleagues going to alter the schedule to extend it for a longer period of time? Just so that I have an idea of how much longer you'd like me to address you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think it would be tidier to take the break now, and resume at 1.40; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: 1.45, I think, Your Honour, on the schedule. But 1.40 is fine too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Then 1.40, an hour and a half from ten past. Okay. Thank you. --- Break taken at 12.10 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours. Paul Rogers, again, appearing on behalf of the Prosecution this afternoon. Your Honours, in response to Mr. Popovic's appeal, the Prosecution observes that, as in his appeal brief, Popovic seeks today to focus on isolated aspects of the evidence, and by so doing to undermine his convictions. But in our submissions, he files address the complex matrix of findings which underlie those convictions and the Chamber 's careful assessment and appreciation of the evidence when making its findings. In our response, I will make some general remarks concerning Popovic's attacks on the Trial Chamber's assessment of the evidence and its approach to the credibility of the witnesses. I will then provide an overview of the basis of Popovic's convictions in order to show how the Trial Chamber's holistic assessment of the evidence inevitably led to the convictions that were entered. After completing my overview, Ms. Soljan will address Your Honours' questions and will make some further remarks concerning Popovic's challenge to his conviction as a member of the JCE to murder and as a genocidaire. And Ms. Nabti will make some submissions on Popovic's genocidal intent. Your Honours, turning then to deal with the assessment of the evidence and the attacks to that. Your Honours, in sum, we have addressed these attacks at length in our response brief, arguing broadly that the Appellant's arguments are unfounded and that the vast majority warrant summary dismissal. Your Honours, of course, we adopt all of the submissions that we have made in response to the Appellant's brief, and you will have recalled, during the course of his submissions, his extensive reference to his own appeal brief in support of the arguments he made today. Your Honours, the appeal of Vujadin Popovic rests primarily on a series of attacks on the Chamber's assessment of the overwhelming evidence in this case against him. In particular, he seeks to undermine the Chamber's assessment of certain witnesses' evidence. For example, he recognises that the assessment of Momir Nikolic's evidence is particularly important because Momir Nikolic places him at the heart of the murder operation from the beginning, from the 12th of July, 1995. And so it is that, again, he repeats his challenges to the reliability and credibility of that witness. Likewise, he recognises that the assessment of Witness PW-168 is also significant because PW-168 implicates Popovic in the murder operation in a number of ways. And so, again, he challenges the reliability and credibility of that witness by repeating his trial arguments and arguing for different interpretations of the evidence. Indeed, wherever evidence implicates him in the murder operation, he reargues his failed case at trial or merely proffers alternative explanations on the evidence without demonstrating why no reasonable Trial Chamber could have reached the conclusion this Chamber did on the totality of the evidence before it. He prefers a piecemeal and isolated assessment of the strands of evidence, ignoring that the Chamber looked at each piece of evidence within the context of the whole of the evidence that it had before it, before reaching its conclusions and drawing inferences and making findings. In doing this, the Chamber demonstrated it had correctly assessed the evidence as a whole, carefully weighing and considering what it was prepared to rely upon and what it was not and giving detailed reasons where appropriate. So to take Momir Nikolic as an example, Popovic does everything he can to argue again why Momir Nikolic should be disbelieved, but he does not address the Chamber's overall approach to the assessment of this evidence and in particular how it assessed his evidence by reference of the applicable standards. Your Honours, the Trial Chamber set out in great detail its approach to the evidence at paragraphs 7 to 85, devoting 23 pages of its judgement to this. It directed itself correctly as to how it must assess the evidence and recognised that it need not assess every factual assertion in the indictment or explain every detail of its assessment of the evidence presented to it in trial judgement at paragraph 15. It correctly noted that where it may not have mentioned a specific piece of evidence, that all relevant evidence had been considered. Again in the judgement at paragraph 15, referring to the Kvocka appeals judgement at paragraph 23. Your Honours, it is trite to say that the assessment of the evidence is supremely within the Trial Chamber's discretion because, of course, that is its primary function. And great deference at this stage of the proceedings is, and I know Your Honours will give great deference to those assessments. It's useful to note at this stage the size of the evidential record in this case. It included over 5.000 exhibits, just under half of which were adduced by the Defence. The Trial Chamber heard 182 Prosecution witnesses over more than 400 days, three-quarters of whom were fully viva voce or with cross-examination via 92 ter, including 12 experts. 145 witnesses were heard from the Defence and the Chamber itself called one witness. The transcript runs into over 34.000 pages excluding closing submissions. The judgement is extensively referenced and footnoted and running into two volumes totalling 866 pages. The Appeals Chamber jurisprudence recognises that the task of assessing this massive material rests with the Trial Chamber. In Lukic and Lukic, in appeals judgement at paragraph 296, Your Honours stated: "The Appeals Chamber recalls that the Trial Chamber has the advantage of observing persons, witnesses in person, and is thus better positioned than the Appeals Chamber to assess the reliability and the credibility of the evidence. It is therefore within the discretion of a Trial Chamber to evaluate discrepancies and to consider the reliability -- consider the credibility of the evidence as a whole without explaining its decision in detail." And footnoted to Kvocka et al, paragraph 23, Celebici appeals judgement paragraphs 481 and 498, and the Kupreskic appeals judgement at paragraph 32. The Appeals Chamber has repeatedly recognised that "the task of hearing, assessing and weighing the evidence presented at trial is left primarily to the Trial Chamber. Thus, the Appeals Chamber must give a margin of deference to a finding of fact reached by a Trial Chamber, and only where the evidence relied upon by the Trial Chamber could not have been accepted by any reasonable Tribunal of fact or where the evaluation of the evidence is wholly erroneous, may the Appeals Chamber substitute its own finding of fact for that of the Trial Chamber." Again Kupreskic appeals judgement paragraph 30; Mrksic appeals judgement paragraph 14; and it's also referred to in Lukic and Lukic appeals judgement.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The counsel is kindly requested to slow down when reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I note the interpreters. The Celebici appeals judgement at paragraph 481 confirms "the Trial Chamber is not required to articulate in its judgement every step of its reasoning in reaching particular findings." It went on: "The Trial Chamber is not obliged to recount and justify its findings in relation to every submission made during trial. It was within its discretion to evaluate the inconsistencies highlighted and to consider whether the witness, when the testimony is taken as a whole, was reliable and whether the evidence was credible." And that final part is from Celebici appeals judgement 498. Your Honours, in this case, the Trial Chamber could not hope to, and nor was it required to, address every piece of evidence. Indeed, as much of the evidence was viva voce, it did not need to assess every difference between witnesses or within a witness's own testimony. However, the Trial Chamber in this case was very careful to articulate in detail its approach to the evidence in general and again specifically when dealing with certain categories of evidence and with certain witnesses and types of witness. In relation to Momir Nikolic, the Trial Chamber addressed its approach to his evidence generally at paragraphs 48 to 53 and specifically with regard to the third Hotel Fontana meeting between paragraphs 280 and 287. Your Honours, it was mindful of all of the Appellant's strong attacks to his credibility. It wasn't just Mr. Popovic who attacked his credibility. Everybody attacked his credibility. And it was mindful of those attacks, including those of Borovcanin, as it listed them in detail in footnote 72. In its assessment, it specifically considered Momir Nikolic's lies made in an effort to secure a plea agreement vis-à-vis the Kravica warehouse at paragraph 49. It considered his attempts on occasion to downplay aspects of his own involvement in the events, paragraph 51, as well as recognition that sometimes he made statements that implicated himself further in the events, in the judgement at paragraph 284, for example, in relation to Nikolic's acceptance that the conversation on the 12th was about the plan to murder and that he, Momir Nikolic, was involved in implementing it by suggesting places of detention and places of execution. It considered specifically his broad consistency, at 52 in the judgement, and his demeanour overall, at paragraph 53. It considered the content of his plea agreement and the statement of facts and acceptance of responsibility, at 281 to 282. It considered whether there was any corroboration of the account given by Momir Nikolic of the 12 July meeting by the events that had happened and, for example, by video evidence placing him there on 12 July, at paragraphs 285, 86, and 87. It considered the testimony of Kosoric, at paragraph 288, and in a detailed explanation in the footnote at 938, it explained how it considered Kosoric was extremely evasive in the questions that were being asked of him and consequently why it rejected his account. It considered whether Momir Nikolic, in the words of the Trial Chamber, "constructed his evidence of this conversation to correspond to the events which subsequently unfolded." And it rejected that as not being a reasonable possibility because the conversation substantially incriminated him in the murder operation at that early stage, judgement 287. It considered other aspects of his evidence such as the corroboration of a meeting between Beara and Deronjic that he talked about in 1269 and 1207, and the corroboration of his own meeting with Drago Nikolic through the evidence of PW-168 whom it also found to be reliable. Your Honours, the Chamber recognised that it did not need to corroborate a witness such as Momir Nikolic - in the judgement at paragraph 26 and also referring to Lukic and Lukic appeals judgement at paragraph 128 - but it expressed its intention to treat that person's evidence with caution, citing at footnote 36 to the Appeals Chamber's jurisprudence from Krajisnik at paragraph 146, where the Appeals Chamber stated: "A Trial Chamber should at least briefly explain why it accepted the evidence of witnesses who may have had motives or incentives to implicate the accused. In this way, a Trial Chamber shows its cautious assessment of the evidence." Your Honours, the Chamber gave detailed reasons for its acceptance of the evidence of Momir Nikolic, where it chose to rely upon him and generally. For example, on the issue of the 12 July conversation with Popovic outside the Hotel Fontana prior to the third meeting, it recognised that Momir Nikolic remained consistent on this subject and on the subject matter discussed at that meeting, despite extensive cross-examination on the point. Trial judgement 282 and footnote 927. Popovic attacks that finding again in his reply brief and he alleges at paragraph 33 that the judgement "corroborated its finding that Nikolic remained consistent despite much cross-examination" by referring to Judge Prost's question regarding Nikolic's evidence, but he misunderstands the nature of that finding and fails to record the other citations referring simply to Judge Prost's question. The Chamber's full citation demonstrates that where Momir Nikolic was examined and cross-examined at length about the content of the conversation, and in particular about the reference to the places of detention and execution, and the places that you can find those discussions and the evidence of the extensive cross-examination is found in the transcript at 32916 to 32918, 32920 on to 32922, 33031 to 34, 33040 to 41, 33043 to 33049, and at 33328. The Trial Chamber decided that Momir Nikolic was credible on the question of the conversation, and its contents and the discussion about the places of execution, at judgement 282. And in particular, it considered the part about detentions and executions was true because this incriminated Momir Nikolic in the organisation of the murder operation, as he was discussing and volunteering places of detention and murder. That's in the judgement at 284. Your Honours, this self-incrimination supported the reliability of the statement as a whole and, in addition, it relied the Chamber on other factors to corroborate the circumstances of the conversation, in judgement at 285, including, for example, the next day when Beara examined the brick factory as a potential place of execution and detention. Referred to in the judgement at 286, 452 to 455, and 460 to 463. And in any event, Momir Nikolic's evidence was not the only evidence from which Popovic's convictions could be sustained. He was inside the Hotel Fontana on the 12th July with Mladic and seen outside of it, judgement 1098 and PW-109. He was staying in the hotel on the nights of 11 and 12 July, corroborated by the hotel receipts referred to in the judgement at 1098. As Drina Corps chief of security he had access to the resources through the Drina Corps brigades, recorded in the judgement at 294, 296, 1069 to 1070, 1094, and 1281 to 1284.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down, please. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: On the evening of the 13th of July, Popovic conveyed to Zvornik -- Drago Nikolic -- to the Zvornik Brigade area, to Drago Nikolic, Mladic's order to execute the prisoners in the Zvornik Brigade area of responsibility, following which Drago Nikolic immediately began working on the new task by leaving the forward command post, being present with the Zvornik Brigade MP commander Jasikovac and others at the Grbavci school on the night of the 13th of July and into the morning of the 14th of July. It's corroborated on the 14th of July, after his 15- to 20-minute meeting at the Standard barracks with Beara and Drago Nikolic, referred to in the judgement at 1106, Popovic accompanied a half-kilometre long column of prisoners and soldiers to the Grbavci school at Orahovac, referred to in the judgement at 1107 and 1108, and he remained present at the school and oversaw the execution, referred to in the judgement at 481, 483 to 488, and 1111 to 1112. And throughout it all, he contributed to ensuring there was sufficient fuel supplies for the work being done, and that's referred to in the judgement at 1110. It also refers to his presence on the 15th of July at the Rocevic school when he sought trucks for transportation of prisoners and personnel to carry out the executions at Kozluk, referred to in the judgement at 511 to 516, and 1118 to 1120.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could counsel kindly slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think I have to make the request explicitly now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm sorry. I'm trying not to go too fast. On the 16th of July, he was present in the Pilica area, directing the 10th Sabotage Detachment members in relation to the executions at Branjevo Farm and also at the Pilica Dom, and continuing to ensure again fuel. And that's referred to in the judgement at 1124 to 1127, and 1130 to 1134. On the 17th of July, he reports the killing and burial operation job, gets an A, trial judgement 1142, and on or about the 23rd of July he facilitated the killing of the 10 Milici prisoners, referred in the judgement at 1153 to 1156. Corroborative of his findings overall -- of the findings overall relating to his involvement in the killing operation is his presence at the Bisina executions on the 23rd of July and, in September 1995, his involvement in the reburial operation, including, again, by obtaining fuel, referred to in the judgement at 1158 to 1161. Your Honours, taking all of that together and the careful assessment of Momir Nikolic's evidence, the Chamber demonstrated that it was very careful in its approach not just towards Momir Nikolic but also to the approach to Witness PW-168. Again, in relation to PW-168, the Trial Chamber gave a detailed explanation of why it considered him to be credible. It's in the judgement at 1347 referring to the judgement at paragraphs 28 to 47. The Chamber was fully cognisant of the many challenges to this witness's reliability, in particular with regard to the conversation between Obrenovic and Drago Nikolic on the night of the 13th July 1995 in which Drago Nikolic informed Obrenovic that Popovic had ordered Drago Nikolic to make preparations for a large number of Bosnian Muslim prisoners coming into the Zvornik sector and that on Mladic's order they were to be shot. It's in the judgement at 1345 to 6. The Chamber gave detailed reasons as to why it accepted PW-168's account, noting much of the content of the conversation was supported by other evidence. It's in the judgement at 1349. For example, in the conversation, Drago Nikolic requested to be relieved from duty at the IKM, forward command post. The fact of his release was supported by the testimony of Mihajlo Galic and the Zvornik Brigade forward command post logbook. And in addition, the evidence of PW-168 that Drago Nikolic, Jasikovac, and members of the Zvornik Brigade MP participated in preparing the detention sites was corroborated by PW-143 and other evidence, the judgement at 1350. Your Honours, this same careful approach is demonstrated by the Chamber's assessment of the evidence of Srecko Acimovic and also in its assessment of PW-101. Your Honours, all of these witnesses testified. Their evidence was received over very many days and subjected to extensive testing through cross-examination. The Trial Chamber was thus in a perfect position to assess the reliability and credibility of the witness. It had the opportunity to observe them, to assess their demeanour, an opportunity not afforded to this Chamber. And indeed, where the Chamber was not sure about evidence implicating Popovic, they rejected it. For example, they rejected evidence of Popovic's presence at the Petkovci dam, in the judgement at 1116. Your Honours, it's trite but this is not a trial de novo. Yet in his challenges to the assessment of the evidence, this is in reality what Popovic seeks. Popovic must fail in his challenges to the approach the Chamber took to the assessment of the witness evidence and the conclusions arising from that approach. Your Honours, I turn now to deal with a broad overview of the JCE to murder. Because of the connections between all of the accused, it's important to understand how the Chamber saw this as a holistic whole in understanding the interrelationships. And as a start, I would like, if I may, please, to just say a few words about the organisational structure of the forces involved in the operation. And, Your Honours, we have created a slide which is fully referenced to the judgement in the bottom left-hand corner you can see, I hope, on your screens, when it comes up. I'll just pause and wait to make sure Your Honours all have it or can at least see one of them. I hope Your Honours can all see it. Tried to make sure the font size is sufficiently large to be -- for our eyes, mine included. The Tribunal should invest in 17- and 21-inch screens but I daren't suggest that. Looking at the slide, what we tried to demonstrate here is the structures on one page so you have an understanding of the connections. The top box shows in broad terms the VRS Main Staff. Doesn't have everybody on it but just the people that are significant for this discussion. At the top, of course, Mladic is the commander, and attached to him is a line to the 65th Protection Regiment. That's there simply to indicate it's one of the units that you've heard about and where it fits. Coming down from Mladic and the first line we see Gvero on the left-hand side for morale, legal, and religious affairs. Obviously previously one of the accused in this case. Then coming along we have Milovanovic, the Chief of Staff, and below him, within the staff sector, sits Mr. Miletic. Then going across to the right-hand side, we see Tolimir as the general responsible for security and intelligence within the Main Staff, and sitting beneath him, Salapura and Beara. And attached to Salapura, the 10th Sabotage Detachment. And then coming down out of the Main Staff to the corps level, which is the middle box, we see how the corps sits. Of course, under the Main Staff are various corps structures, the Drina Corps being the relevant one here. See the command is there marked as Zivanovic and General Krstic. Of course, Krstic replacing Zivanovic on the 13th of July. Then on the left-hand side, Borovcanin sits as a temporary attachment to the Drina Corps, and to the right-hand side sits Popovic, obviously with others, but that's the connection as chief of security in the Drina Corps. And then we move down below to the brigade levels and on the left-hand side the Bratunac Brigade. Sitting in the Bratunac Brigade is Blagojevic as the commander, Momir Nikolic as the security organ within the Bratunac Brigade. Of course, it's helpful to understand who he is and where he sits as we hear so much about him. And then there is a reference to Jankovic as the commander of the military police. Moving across to the Zvornik Brigade, we see its commander, Vinko Pandurevic, and then sitting below him is Obrenovic, the Chief of Staff. And going through the Chief of Staff, Jokic, the engineering commander, and Jasikovac, the military police commander. And then sitting to the right-hand side, Drago Nikolic, the security organ within the Zvornik Brigade. And Your Honours see the dotted line joining the security organs representing their professional reporting line, it's a dotted line, not a solid line, but it represents their professional reporting line. And how they are connected together at least in that regard. I hope that gives some useful insight at least on one page as to how the structures fit together. As the judgement found, the murder operation was "a coordinated effort reaching from the VRS commander," Mladic, "and some members of the Main Staff through the Drina Corps, the MUP and down to the Zvornik and Bratunac Brigades and the battalions thereof." They went on: "... it is clear that individual units from across the VRS worked together in the implementation of the common purpose." Judgement 1065. Your Honours, I think we can remove the structure from the screen if that's distracting. They went on: "Further, what is clear is from the evidence before the Trial Chamber is that such an operation, on a massive scale, involving the participation of a multitude of VRS members from the Main Staff down, could not have been undertaken absent the authorisation and order of the VRS commander Mladic," judgement 1071. It concluded: "The Trial Chamber is satisfied that Mladic was a driving -- a central, driving force behind the plan to murder and its implementation." Judgement 1071. Your Honours, in order to implement this order on such a massive scale, the Trial Chamber recognised that the concerted effort from many was needed. And in relation to the security administration, it recognised: "... while various battalion, brigade and corps commanders, forces and individual members were drawn into the plan as participants and perpetrators, each contributing in different ways, this was an operation steadily organised and directed by the security branch of the VRS." Judgement 1070. Your Honours, with ruthless efficiency, the forces of the Drina Corps, including MUP units and in particular the Zvornik Brigade, have been mobilised to exterminate a thousand men at Kravica warehouse on the 13th of July, between 800 and 2 and a half thousand at Orahovac on the 14th of July, over 1800 men at Petkovci and Kozluk on the 15th of July, and between a thousand and 2.000 in the Pilica area on the 16th of July. One day later, on the 17th of July, the bodies had been removed from site and buried. Within five days, those fathers, brothers and sons had simply vanished. We agree with Vujadin Popovic when he argues at paragraph 181 of his brief "the highest echelons of the Main Staff could not have any preconceived plan to commit mass murder without resolving the most basic logistics, at least, one, when, two, where, and three, who would carry it out. And that at paragraph 182 when he says: "Further, this plan required various resources, manpower, ammunition, vehicles, machines, and fuel." We agree. It did. The operation required massive coordination and cooperation between many forces on the ground. The Trial Chamber found that in relation to this, Popovic played a pivotal role in the organisation, coordination and implementation of the killing operation, judgement 1168. It found as for Beara that he played a key role in orchestrating the murder operation by planning, coordinating, and overseeing the detention, execution and burial of the victims, judgement 1299. Together, Popovic and Beara organised other security officers to assist including Drago Nikolic and Momir Nikolic, judgement 1068. In Zvornik area, Popovic, Beara and Drago Nikolic worked closely together to translate the murder plan into actions by their planning and physical preparations, judgement 1391 to 2. But their organisation would come to nothing without the use of the brigade assets and the support of the brigade and the corps commanders. This is illustrated by the need for Drago Nikolic to obtain permission from Obrenovic, Chief of Staff of the Zvornik Brigade, to be released from duty at the IKM of the Zvornik Brigade to implement the murder plan, and for permission to use brigade assets, in this case Jasikovac and the MP. It's found in the judgement at 1345. Likewise, Beara, a Main Staff officer with the security administration, reporting directly to Tolimir, the Main Staff general, needed to obtain additional troops from Krstic, the Drina Corps commander, on the 15th of July, to distribute 3500 parcels which the Chamber found was a euphemism for the killing of the prisoners, as demonstrated by the intercepted conversation with Krstic on the 15th of July and referred to in the judgement at 1282. The fact that so many were killed in such a short space of time and their bodies dumped into mass graves is a testament to the ruthless efficiency of the killing operation operated by Popovic, Beara and Nikolic and supported logistically by the Zvornik and Bratunac Brigades. Without their guards, their transport, their munitions, without those willing to kill, without their machinery and the men to bury the bodies, this operation could not have been successful. The fact there were but a handful of survivors shows the calculated determination to eliminate every last one of the victims, to make sure that the details of this terrible crime could never come to light. Thankfully, miraculously, some survived, some hidden under the corpses of friends and brothers, some managing to escape and live despite terrible wounds. Their voices were heard, together with the voices of those who carried out the killings, those who buried the bodies, those who organised the logistics, and testified to the organisation. Together, the Trial Chamber was able to build a clear picture of what happened on those notorious days between the 11th and the 17th of July, 1995, and in relation to the cover-up in the months that followed. Your Honours, I turn now to the events of the 11th to the 17th of July and how the team of Popovic and Beara and Nikolic accomplished the killings. Your Honours, let me first give a short outline of the events leading up to the formation of the murder plan. 11th of July, Srebrenica fell, judgement 260. Thousands of Bosnian Muslims fled from Srebrenica to Potocari, judgement 264. As they fled the enclave they were shelled and shot at, judgement 265. On the evening of the 11th of July, many able-bodied men gathered at Susnjari, having separated from their families on the road to Potocari, as they feared they would be killed if they remained in the Srebrenica enclave once it fell into Bosnian Serb hands, judgement 267. A fear that was evidently well-founded. Before midnight, a column of 10- to 15.000 men formed between Susnjari and Jaglici approximately ten kilometres long and started to move towards Konjevic Polje via Nova Kasaba and on to Tuzla, judgement 269. The column presented a significant challenge for the VRS forces in Bratunac and Zvornik, and on the 11th of July, VRS forces were ordered to block it and carry out ambush activities on it, judgement 364. Your Honours, I'll just ask you to look now at a map. This is Exhibit P02111. I just want to orientate you around the region, so if the places are not fully familiar, at least they may become familiar. Your Honours can see on the map, and towards the bottom, Srebrenica, and if we drive up the road from Srebrenica towards Potocari, going north, we can see coming from Potocari to the left is a little road towards Jaglici and Susnjari. Does Your Honours have that on the screen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I believe we need some help.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Ah, forgive me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Please start over.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes. If I can just orientate Your Honours, if I make sure all of Your Honours have got it now, yes. Thank you. If we go to Srebrenica, down at the bottom, the large town or large words of the town, then we can find it, and then drive north, imagine we are on a road driving north and we come a fork in the road and there is Potocari. Now we can carry on north to Bratunac or we can turn left just before Potocari and drive in our car towards Jaglici and Susnjari. And there, you will see two red lines. And the two red lines travel northwest towards Nova Kasaba, if you follow them you will arrive at Nova Kasaba and Konjevic Polje. That indicates the direction of movement of the column, from -- when it started to move towards Konjevic Polje. And if we get to Konjevic Polje, Nova Kasaba, and then drive back towards Bratunac on the road, we will drive through Sandici, Kravica and Glogova, and then finally we arrive back in Bratunac. So, Your Honours, just having orientated you around the locations, I just want to speak now a little bit about the 12th of July and I'll come back to the map in a minute. Your Honours, the 12th of July was about the separation of the remaining men from the women and children in Potocari. Women and children were bussed away and the men detained. In addition, orders were given on the 12th to secure the Konjevic Polje to Bratunac road, from the column of the Muslim men seeking to break through to Tuzla. That's in judgement 365. The Chamber found that the murder operation began on the 12th July with the separation of the men from the Bosnian women and children gathered in Potocari, at judgement 1050. Buses and trucks to transport the civilians away began to arrive in the afternoon, judgement 316, arranged on the orders of Mladic on the 11th of July. 293 in the judgement. The men were separated by Bratunac Brigade MPs supervised by Momir Nikolic, the security organ for the Bratunac Brigade in whose area of responsibility at that time the prisoners were held. Sometime before the third Hotel Fontana meeting that morning, Popovic told Momir Nikolic that these separated men were all to be killed. Momir Nikolic, using his local knowledge, assisted Popovic, Drina Corps security chief, with identifying locations to detain and also to execute prisoners. He identified the Vuk Karadzic school and the hangar in Bratunac, both locations where hundreds of prisoners were subsequently held. Popovic argues in his brief and again today that Nikolic's account of this meeting should be rejected, that he was unclear and inconsistent about whether he suggested detention and execution sites or whether only Popovic or Kosoric mentioned it, in his appeal brief at 75 to 77. But the Trial Chamber was clear that it considered Nikolic remained consistent in his account of the discussion and the content of that discussion on the morning of the 12th July outside the Hotel Fontana and, as I've already outlined, gave detailed reasons why it accepted his evidence, 280 to 288. The Chamber carefully analysed his statement of facts from the 6th of May, 2003, and indeed made it an exhibit in the case, Exhibit C1.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down for the purposes of interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I think you have to make a more determined effort.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: I'm trying, Your Honour. I'm sorry. I usually run into [indiscernible]. Your Honours, to resume the narrative, the separated men were detained at the White House in Potocari on both the 12th and the 13th of July, guarded by Bosnian Serb forces including MUP and VRS soldiers. In Potocari, some men made it on to buses with the women and children, going towards Kladanj to the west. But at Tisca, the buses were stopped, VRS soldiers searched them, removed the men, and on one occasion 70 or 80 were taken away in the direction of the forest. And later, on the 13th of July, around 20 men were separated at Luke near Tisca and that night taken to a field and shot in the back of the truck, the sole survivor fleeing into the forest. He had heard the soldiers discussing Kravica and how "they had finished with the balijas." Returning to Potocari, eventually the men from the White House were transported to Bratunac. We will just return now to the map. We have animated just to show you the movement, from Potocari to Bratunac. In Bratunac, they were, as I've described already, held in various locations where they were guarded by Bosnian Serb forces. We will just keep the map there because I'll return to it in a minute. On the night of 12/13 July, elements of the column attacked VRS forces along the road. That's the Bratunac to Konjevic Polje road. Turning now into the 13th of July, in summary, this was a day when the prisoners were being transported to the Bratunac area and detained to await their fate. It was a day also when the killings began: At Kravica warehouse, a thousand; in Cerska Valley, 150; Jadar River, 16. Bratunac was to be the collection point for the majority of the prisoners. The executions were originally planned to be nearby, but the plan had to change, resulting in the transportation of prisoners to the Zvornik area of responsibility. On the 13th of July, a fresh order from the VRS Main Staff to the Drina Corps, Zvornik, and other brigades, was issued to block, disarm and capture Muslim groups and prevent them from crossing into Muslim territory, judgement 379. As part of that initiative, Bosnian Serb forces issued an ultimatum to members of the column to surrender or be killed. As a result, thousands surrendered. They were initially detained at various sites at Konjevic Polje area including the Sandici meadow and at Nova Kasaba. And an intercept timed at 5.30 p.m. on the 13th of July indicates over 6.000 men were being held at three locations in the Bratunac area. Your Honours, to continue with the arrow sequence, just want to show you some of the movements. There was an intersection between Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road to Nova Kasaba. If you find the Konjevic Polje there in the north-west, there was a small movement to a warehouse in Konjevic Polje. It's referred to in the judgement at 389. Also on the 13 of July, from the warehouse in Konjevic Polje, there was a movement to the Nova Kasaba football field. Also, on the 13th, at Sandici, so to just travel along the road towards Sandici, please, on the Bratunac road, you'll find there is a movement from there to the Kravica warehouse. It's in the judgement at 388 and 421. Also from Sandici to Bratunac, referred to in the judgement at 388. Back to Konjevic Polje, from the warehouse in Konjevic Polje to Bratunac, judgement 389. And finally, from the Nova Kasaba football field to Bratunac, so south of Konjevic Polje there is a movement there. So Your Honours can see, on the 13th of July, there is a collection of prisoners broadly in the Bratunac area. There is a number of common themes relating to them which demonstrate that they were marked to be killed. For the most part, they were not fed or provided with adequate water or access to medical facilities. No adequate records, apart from a few, were made of their existence. Names and details were not taken in relation to the detention of the prisoners. There was some evidence of that but not for the vast majority. Their personal belongs were piled up, identity documents were removed, money and gold were stolen from them. They were held in appalling conditions, overcrowded and insanitary. They were abused. They were insulted. And for many they were bound, they were blindfolded, and then they were murdered. On the night of the 13th of July, Beara, in Bratunac, announced himself to Deronjic as the man who had "come to kill all the Bosnian Muslims that were being warehoused in schools and buses in Bratunac." Judgement 1264. But the reaction of the local SDS was that the killings were not to be carried out in the Bratunac area and there was an argument. Judgement 1264 and 1270. New locations were needed. But by this time, the Kravica warehouse killings had already happened in the late afternoon of the 13th of July, so there was already a burial problem. Solutions for the burials of the dead were debated through the early hours of the 14th, resulting in Beara ordering PW-161 later to go with an MP to find a place to bury the Kravica bodies. They did. They were buried at Glogova and Ravnice. And. In order to solve the problem of continued executions, the Zvornik Brigade became involved as new places of detention and murder away from Bratunac were required. That evening, on the 13th of July, Beara ordered Momir Nikolic to go to the Zvornik Brigade forward command post to tell Drago Nikolic that Bosnian Muslim prisoners were to be detained and killed in the Zvornik area. Drago Nikolic called Obrenovic, the Chief of Staff of the Zvornik Brigade, to be asked to be relieved of duty at the IKM so that he could make preparations for prisoners from Bratunac who were to be brought to the Zvornik Brigade area of responsibility and killed. Nikolic told Obrenovic -- Momir Nikolic told Obrenovic -- sorry, Drago Nikolic told Obrenovic that Popovic had called him and asked him to make arrangements and that Popovic and Beara would bring the prisoners. Nikolic also asked to be given Jasikovac and a company of MP for the task. Your Honours can find it this in the judgement around 1345. That evening, on the 13th of July, Zvornik Brigade MP under the command of Jasikovac went to the Grbavci school to begin preparations to receive prisoners. Drago Nikolic was at the school that night giving orders to the MP there to guard the prisoners, and prisoners arrived from Bratunac. The 14th of July, Popovic, Nikolic and were working together to transport and detain the prisoners and coordinated their murders. Popovic and Nikolic coordinated the transport, detention and murder, and throughout the day and night, burials of the dead continued. The last map I'll show you on the slide, please, indicates just in broad terms, between the 14th and 16 July, the movements of the prisoners from Bratunac up north to the places where they were killed. So starting with the arrow on the left, after it splits, the arrowhead ends Orahovac. The second arrowhead ends at Petkovci. And then there is a movement from the Petkovci school to the dam shown by the little arrow. The third arrowhead ends in Rocevic, and there is a movement to Kozluk. And the final arrowheads split to the Kula school at Branjevo, near Branjevo, and Pilica Dom, the cultural centre, and the movement from the Kula school to Branjevo Farm. Obviously, the arrow doesn't indicate precisely where they physically went. It's not suggesting for a moment this that they went through the territory of the FRY. It's just indicative of the movement of the prisoners north over the 14th, 15th, and into the 16th. So on the 14th of July in the morning, at around 8.00 a.m., Nikolic, Popovic and Beara meet at the Standard barracks, that is the Zvornik Brigade headquarters in Karakaj. And Karakaj is just to the west -- to the east of Orahovac, north of Zvornik. The Chamber found that that meeting concerned the murder operation, judgement 472. Following that, Beara returned to Bratunac in order to attend to the task of burying the dead from the Kravica murders and finding places to detain and murder other prisoners. And after the meeting, Popovic left to accompany the convoy of prisoners from Bratunac. In Bratunac, Popovic led the convoy, judgement 1108, to the Grbavci school in Orahovac, stopping in Divic to pick up Drago Nikolic. Popovic was in Orahovac as the prisoners were herded into the school. Drago Nikolic was seen throughout the day in Orahovac directing operations as between 800 and 2500 prisoners were detained there, moved to a field about a kilometre up the road and murdered. And in the afternoon of the 14th of July, Zvornik Brigade engineers and excavators were digging a large pit at Orahovac at the execution site, in judgement 482. The prisoners were kept in appalling conditions in the school, they were blindfolded, they were bound before being herded on to the trucks and driven to their deaths. 481 to 484. Soldiers from the 4th Battalion Zvornik Brigade and logistics personnel escorted the prisoners to the site, 483. And trucks, including Zvornik Brigade trucks, transported the prisoners throughout the afternoon and the evening --

utterances.text: Can the counsel please slow down? It's impossible.
