utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you. I have to lose some weight first, I think, but thank you. At least one member of the 4th Battalion participated in the killings. The Trial Chamber found that both Drago Nikolic and Popovic were present during the killings at Orahovac and were directing those killings. Judgement 1112. As the Orahovac killings were taking place, a new request for digging equipment was made to the Zvornik Brigade in relation to the task "being performed by Popovic and Beara." That's found in the judgement at 1277. And Beara was seen at the Grbavci school in Orahovac. He was also seen at the school near Nova Kasaba football field and, later that afternoon, back at the Zvornik Brigade headquarters at the Standard barracks where he was complaining: "We have a lot of prisoners and it's very hard for us to control them. They are at various locations in the Zvornik municipality. We have to get rid of them. I expect assistance from the municipality." Judgement 1278. By this assistance, the Chamber found he meant to get rid of the dead; that is, to kill them and bury their bodies. Beara said he was in command of the barracks and that the orders came from "the two presidents," judgement 1278. Jokic, the engineering man, called Beara at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters complaining that there were big problems with the parcels, meaning prisoners, judgement 1280. The Zvornik Brigade notebook records at 3.00 p.m., "Colonel Beara is coming in (the following) order, to Orovoc," that is Orahovac, "Petkovci, Rocevic, and Pilica." Judgement 1276. Later that evening, Beara was seen at the Petkovci school with Drago Nikolic, judgement 1279, and the Chamber found that Beara coordinated the detention, transport, execution, and burial of the prisoners detained at Petkovci. Meanwhile, also on the 14th of July, other prisoners were being moved to the Kula school near Pilica and to the Rocevic school near Kozluk. Drago Nikolic, as well as his involvement in the operation at Orahovac, was in contact with the 1st Battalion Zvornik Brigade asking Slavko Peric, the assistant commander for security intelligence, to go to the Kula school to ensure there were no problems with local civilians. Ten to 15 members of the 1st Battalion then went to the school to secure it for the arrival of the prisoners, judgement 527. Prisoners arrived and were again detained in the school in abysmal overcrowded, insanitary conditions. Food and water were scarce. No medical treatment was provided. Prisoners were beaten if they wanted to use a toilet and so they soiled themselves, judgement 529. Guarding by the 1st Battalion continued throughout the day and night of the 14th, 15th, and into the 16th. At Rocevic school, Bosnian Muslim prisoners were detained and guarded by Bratunac Brigade soldiers including MP, and between the 14th and 15th of July, those numbers swelled to around a thousand, judgement 1117. And in the afternoon of the 14th, Srecko Acimovic, commander of the 2nd Battalion, called the Zvornik Brigade headquarters and spoke there to Popovic about the prisoners. Popovic said they would be exchanged the next day. Judgement 1113. Moving into the 15th, Popovic, Beara and Nikolic continued to work together to ensure the killing operation continued at pace. The burials at Orahovac continued and the killings at Kozluk of the prisoners from Rocevic began and the killings of the Petkovci school detainees also started. In the early hours of the 15th, Drago Nikolic was acting as the duty officer at the Zvornik Brigade. A message was sent from the Zvornik Brigade headquarters to Acimovic, the 2nd Battalion commander, to form a platoon to be sent to Rocevic to kill the prisoners there. At about 0230, Nikolic followed up the telegram insisting that the order be carried out, judgement 1368. When Acimovic refused, Nikolic said he would meet Acimovic that morning at the school, and reported that Beara was coming to the Standard barracks at around 9.00 a.m. At around 10.00, Popovic met Acimovic at the school. Popovic was angry, asking why the executions squad had not been brought as ordered, judgement 511 and 1118. He was angry when only one truck turned up to transport the prisoners to the execution site, saying that they would have to be killed at the school. Judgement 513. Acimovic ordered the prisoners to be taken to Kozluk where ultimately they were killed by the 2nd Battalion Zvornik Brigade, including at least one MP. They were guarded by the 2nd Battalion MPs. They were blindfolded and bound and loaded on to 2nd Battalion trucks, 518, and transported to the killing site at Kozluk. Three crates of ammunition for automatic rifles were sent to the Rocevic school by the 2nd Battalion, and one of the 2nd Battalion soldiers testified of the prisoners: "They were half dead, exhausted, without water or bread, nobody, nobody begged for their lives. And this worries me greatly. Nobody said, 'Spare my life.'" Judgement 518. The prisoners were shot on the banks of the river. That morning, around 10.00 a.m., Beara called Krstic asking for ten -- 15 to 30 men to help in the murder operation. He told Krstic he had 3500 parcels to distribute, in other words to kill, and he couldn't do anything without the additional men. He was told to take soldiers from the Bratunac Brigade, judgement 1282. There were still around 3.000 men distributed between Rocevic, Kula school, and the Pilica cultural centre. Meanwhile, still on the 15th, the burials at Orahovac continued with Zvornik Brigade engineering assets, and trucks were being used to remove prisoners and bodies from the Petkovci school. Those detained at the Petkovci school were told to remove most of their clothes, had their personal materials taken from them. They were blindfolded and bound, loaded on to 6th Battalion Zvornik Brigade trucks, transported to the Petkovci dam killing field and murdered. In the evening, Popovic and Beara met at the Zvornik Brigade headquarters. By the 16th of July, only the Kula school and the Pilica Dom cultural centre prisoners remained to be killed, the last stretch in the operation, between a thousand and 2.000. Beara and Popovic, the judgement found, arrived at the Kula school around noon that day with around 10 to 12 soldiers in a van and an empty bus. Soon after, the prisoners were bound, some were blindfolded, they were driven away, taken to the Branjevo military farm, a Zvornik Brigade asset, and in groups of ten they were murdered. The killing was undertaken by eight to ten men of the 10th Sabotage Detachment and continued from 10.00 in the morning until 3 or 4 in the afternoon when the killers were joined by soldiers from Bratunac. One survivor testified: "When they opened fire, I threw myself onto the ground. My hands were still tied behind my back and I fell on my stomach, face down. And one man fell on my head. I think he was killed on the spot. And I could feel the hot blood pouring over me. The shooting continued and then they ordered soldiers to shoot people individually. And I could hear a voice saying that they shouldn't shoot people in the heads, so that their brains wouldn't spill out, but rather to shoot them in their backs." Judgement 539. The Trial Chamber found that Popovic was the lieutenant colonel who arrived at the farm in the morning in company with two MPs and the 10th Sabotage execution squad, judgement 1131 to 33. A short distance away at the Pilica cultural centre of all places, prisoners had been brought a few days earlier. They were guarded by Bosnian Serb forces. And in the afternoon, they were all murdered there in the cultural centre. Popovic was in the area at that time, according to the judgement, ordering 500 litres of fuel to be delivered to Pilica "or else," as recorded in an intercept at 1.58 p.m. on the 16th, "the work he's doing will stop. The Trial Chamber rightly considered that this fuel was related to the transport, execution, and burial of the prisoners. A lieutenant colonel also ordered men from the 10th Sabotage to go to the Dom, the cultural centre, from Branjevo Farm to kill the prisoners. Judgement found this was Popovic. 540, 1133. He had been in the cafe at Pilica a few metres from the Dom, the judgement found, and a soldier reported to him after the killings there that "everything is finished." Judgement 1133. When the Branjevo Farm executions and the Pilica Dom killings completed everything was finished. The prisoners were all dead. At about 9.16 p.m. that evening, Popovic is intercepted reporting: "Tell the general ... I've finished the job ... I finished everything." Intercept P01201A, judgement 1136. The only thing to be done after the killing was the burying of the bodies, and on the 17th of July, Popovic reported, the judgement found, on the satisfactory completion of the murder operation. The burials were completed on the 17th, the judgement found, between 542 to 547, with engineers and equipment from the Zvornik Brigade. And in the afternoon of the 17th, Popovic reported: "Everything is okay, that job is done ... everything's been brought to an end, no problems ... basically that gets an A ... an A ... the grade is an A" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you, Mr. Rogers. I'm informed by my colleague that the French interpreters are not able to follow you because of your speed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm nearly finished, you'll be pleased to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not surprising.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, just to conclude with this: I'll just reread this part. In the afternoon of the 17th, Popovic reported: "Everything is okay, that job is done ... everything's been brought to an end, no problems ... basically that gets an A ... an A ... the grade is an A, everything's okay." It's the intercept at 4.22 p.m., P01224A, judgement 1142. And the Trial Chamber found that the job that was being referred to was not anything innocent but was the murder and burial operation. But Popovic's work was not quite complete. On the 23rd of July, after the main killings between the 13th and 16th, a sweep operation was put in place throughout the Zvornik Brigade area of responsibility and elsewhere in the Zvornik and Srebrenica area. Ten Bosnian Muslim wounded prisoners had been taken to the Milici hospital and, on the 23rd of July, they were transferred to the Standard barracks. Pandurevic sought advice from the Drina command as to what to do. In itself revealing. Popovic was duly dispatched from the corps command, the judgement found, 1153. The patients were taken away and they were never seen again. PW-168 testified that Obrenovic had been told by Pandurevic that Popovic had arrived with an order from Mladic for the injured men to be liquidated and they were driven away. Trial Chamber also found on the same day of the Milici patient killings that Popovic was involved in the mass killings at Bisina, when prisoners were taken five at a time from trucks and shot. Judgement 1143 to 1152. And finally, in September 1995, the Chamber found Popovic was involved in the reburial operation of the bodies at Glogova, which the Chamber rightly considered as corroborative of his role in the murder operation, judgement 1161. Your Honours, in conclusion, Popovic was in it from the beginning. He was in Potocari on the 12th of July explaining the murder plan before the separations began on the 13th. He enlisted VRS members such as Momir Nikolic, Drago Nikolic, and Srecko Acimovic to accomplish the plan. He organised and led the transportation of prisoners to the Grbavci school at Orahovac. He was present at many of the places of detention, including Rocevic and the Kula school. The Chamber found he was at Branjevo Farm and close by the Pilica cultural centre. He organised fuel for the killings, transport, and executioners. He reported on the success of the work he had done and participated in its cover-up through the reburial of those murdered. He was committed and dedicated to the task he had been given. He was rightly and justly convicted for his major role in this atrocity, and his appeals must be dismissed. Your Honours, this completes my overview and my submissions. And I will pass over, I suspect after the break, to Ms. Soljan and Ms. Nabti.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Your suspicion is right. We will take a break now and resume in 20 minutes. --- Break taken at 3.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, counsel, as far as your pace is concerned, think of it as in horse racing terms, not a gallop but somewhere between a trot and a gallop, a canter. I think that would serve us well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, message understood. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everybody. My name is Lada Soljan and I'm here on behalf of the Prosecution today. Your Honours, in my submission today, I will briefly summarise Popovic's whereabouts during the relevant time period, to demonstrate how omnipresent he was in the Bratunac and Zvornik Brigade areas of responsibility from the day that Srebrenica fell. By doing this, I aim to address his overarching challenge that he was just a security officer who was not authorised to coordinate and who was simply carrying out his regular duties while the thousands of Bosnian Muslim men and boys were being executed. As argued in our response brief, the only reasonable conclusion based on many strands of interconnecting and mutually corroborating evidence - the conclusion that the Trial Chamber reached - is that Popovic significantly contributed to the murder operation through his robust and vigorous participation. This is at judgement 1178 and 1180. He was properly convicted for persecutions, murder, extermination, and genocide on this basis. Finally, Your Honours, I shall respond to your questions in relation to the Kozluk gravesite. As for the rest, the Prosecution stands by its written submissions. I will of course be happy to answer any questions that you may have. Your Honours, you should be seeing on your screens an exhibit, a map, this is Exhibit P2110, same exhibit as Mr. Rogers showed earlier, and I would like to use it to highlight some aspects of Popovic's participation in the murder plan, in other words, to show how ubiquitous he was from the fall of Srebrenica to less than a week later, when thousands of Bosnian Muslim men and boys lay buried in the Bratunac and Zvornik Brigade areas of responsibility. Your Honours, any addition to the original map is based entirely upon the finding in the judgement and it's reflected by the trial judgement paragraphs therein. So on the 11th of July, Your Honours, Popovic was seen walking with General Mladic and other senior VRS officers through the empty streets of Srebrenica town. On 12 July, he was outside the Hotel Fontana in Bratunac, prior to the third Hotel Fontana meeting. This is where he told Momir Nikolic "all the balija have to be killed" and discovered possible detention sites -- and discussed possible detention sites and execution sites in the area. Judgement 1097. Popovic attended the third and final Hotel Fontana meeting at which the separations and screening of war criminals were mentioned, and he was also present with Bosnian Serb forces in Potocari throughout that day on the 12th. Your Honours, on the 13th of July, Popovic attended a meeting at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters with Mladic, Vasic and General Krstic. Around this time, Mladic angrily confronted Popovic outside the headquarters over his perception that Popovic was not getting on with his work. This is at trial judgement 1100. That evening, at around 7 or 8 p.m., Popovic called Drago Nikolic and informed him that a large number of prisoners were to be brought from Bratunac to Zvornik to be killed and he asked Nikolic to assist. Trial judgement 1104 and 1345. The next morning, Your Honours, on July 14, Popovic was at a short 15- to 20-minute meeting in Standard barracks with both Beara and Drago Nikolic. In light of the timing of this meeting, the position of these three individuals, as well as their prior and subsequent actions, the Trial Chamber reasonably found that the meeting concerned the organisation and coordination of the murder operation, at trial judgement 472. After the meeting, Popovic went to Bratunac, from which he led a large convoy consisting of VRS soldiers and Bosnian Muslim prisoners to Grbavci school in Orahovac. A large pit was dug in a field a short distance away from the school and machine operators were requested to go to Orahovac "in relation to the task being performed by Beara and Popovic." The Chamber found that between 800 and 2500 Bosnian Muslim men were executed at Orahovac that day and that, in light of the totality of the evidence, there was no other reasonable conclusion but that Popovic was at Orahovac on 14 July and directed the executions there. Your Honours, we have fully briefed the issue of PW-101, the witness who places a lieutenant colonel at this execution site. We've done this in our response brief at paragraphs 169 to 190.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's the gallop not the canter.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: I'll go back to a trot if I can. In addition, we have made further submissions regarding PW-101 in our response to the sixth Popovic Rule 115 motion. Your Honours, by the evening of 14 July, Bosnian Muslim men were detained inside both Rocevic and Kula schools under similar conditions as the prisoners at Grbavci school had been, and Popovic had a telephone discussion with Acimovic concerning the prisoners there. The next morning, 15 July, Popovic was at Rocevic school. He was coordinating the execution of prisoners, he was procuring trucks from Standard barracks to take the prisoners to the execution site, and he was attempting to engage Zvornik Brigade soldiers and volunteers to shoot them. Judgement 511 to 517. The Chamber found that over 1.000 prisoners were executed at Kozluk that day, based on eyewitness testimony and forensic evidence. Your Honours, in his briefs, as well as today, Popovic challenges the Chamber's reliance on Acimovic in reaching its findings regarding his coordination of on-site logistics for the executions of the Rocevic school prisoners at Kozluk. We stand by our response brief at paragraphs 198 to 217. Around 6.30 p.m. that evening, Popovic again met Beara at the Standard barracks. Meanwhile, 1.000 to 2.000 prisoners had been detained in the Pilica area, judgement 1124. On the 16th of July, Your Honours, Popovic was seen at the Zvornik Brigade headquarters and he joined, together with two MPs, members of a 10th Sabotage Unit, which had been ordered to execute busloads of Bosnian Muslims at the Branjevo military farm. Popovic arrived at the Kula school with Beara around noon and, upon his arrival, the prisoners were driven to Branjevo military farm and executed. The Chamber found that around 3 to 4 p.m., a lieutenant colonel, in other words, Popovic, obtained volunteers who were deployed at the Branjevo military farm to go to the Pilica Dom to execute the 500 Bosnian Muslims detained there and they then left with Popovic and the two MPs. Between 1.000 to 2.000 Bosnian Muslims were executed in Pilica and Branjevo Farm and the Pilica cultural centre on 16 July. Your Honours, in his appeal brief and again today at transcript references pages 21 to 23, Popovic disputes the findings that he coordinated logistics on site and that he was the lieutenant colonel present in the Pilica area on June -- on 16 July. He does so primarily by attacking Erdemovic's inability to identify Popovic as well as by advancing numerous speculative and piecemeal alternative interpretations of evidence. However, as developed in our response, paragraphs 218 to 228, the Chamber has reasonably based its findings on the totality of mutually reinforcing pieces of evidence before concluding that the identification was objectively reliable. Specifically, the Chamber took into account his rank, lieutenant colonel. It took into account the fact that no other lieutenant colonel was present in the area at that time. It reasonably took into account his movements during the 16th of July in the Pilica area, including, first, his presence at the Kula school at noon together with Beara, and then later, the fact that a note in the Zvornik Brigade duty officer logbook at 4.40 indicated that he was in the Pilica area at that time, around the time of the Branjevo executions. The Trial Chamber also took into account his prior role in coordinating the executions in Orahovac and in Rocevic. The Chamber further relied on evidence concerning his requisition of fuel, including the 1.58 p.m. intercept that Popovic urgently required 500 litres of fuel to be delivered to Pilica "or else the work he's doing will stop," and a contemporaneous note at 2.00 p.m. in the Zvornik Brigade duty officer logbook that Popovic requested a bus with a full tank and 500 litres of D2. The Chamber reasonably found that even a later intercept at 7.12 p.m. concerning "the request that Zvornik sent" referred to the delivery of fuel. This is at judgement 1128. And it considered the evidence of driver Branko Bogicevic, that he indeed transported 500 litres of fuel from Standard barracks to Pilica on the same day. Additionally, his vehicle log indicated he had travelled to Pilica that day. Based on all this mutually corroborating evidence, Your Honours, the Chamber reasonably found that Popovic's request for fuel and its delivery were related to the operation of executing and burying the prisoners at Branjevo military farm. Later that night, Your Honours, at 9.16 p.m., Popovic was intercepted on a call he made from the Standard barracks in which he stated: "I've finished the job." Taking into account all of the evidence and Popovic's activities in the days leading up to this conversation, the Trial Chamber concluded that the only reasonable interpretation of this evidence is that "the job" refers to the killing operation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Slow down, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, as Mr. Rogers has already indicated, the job referred to in the intercept you have before you for the 17th of July refers to the operation to kill and bury the Bosnian Muslim men in Zvornik between 13 and 17 July. It is Popovic's report that the job gets an A. Your Honours, the Chamber found that Popovic killed or facilitated the killing of ten wounded Bosnian Muslim prisoners from Milici hospital who were placed in his custody around 23 July. This is at judgement 577 and 1156. The Defence repeated its prior challenges here about the underlying -- for the basis of this finding. Again piecemeal. This finding was based on evidence besides just witness testimony, this finding was based on the evidence of two intercepted conversations on that day, which mentioned that Popovic would arrive to sort the matter out, as well as a contemporaneous note in the Zvornik Brigade duty officer logbook that: "8.30 hours - Lieutenant Colonel Cerovic relayed message from commander that LTC Popovic will arrive by 1700 hours." This is at judgement 1153 and footnote 3761. There was also testimony that Popovic had arrived with an order from Mladic for the injured men to be liquidated and that they were driven away, as well as vehicle log records that the car assigned to Popovic had travelled from Vlasenica to Zvornik. Judgement 1154 and 1155. The Chamber also found he had been involved with and present during the executions of prisoners at Bisina. It concluded that his presence at the Bisina execution site and his participation in the reburial operation in September of 1995 corroborated his participation in the JCE to murder. Judgement 1161 and 1166. Your Honours, in paragraphs 84, 88, 93 to 97, and 232 to 238 of the Prosecution response brief, we address Popovic's arguments challenging the conclusion that he and the security branch played a key role in organising and directing the murder operation. Your Honours, Popovic was not a powerless security officer with no authority and no access to personnel or resources, as he has been arguing both at trial and now on appeal. On the contrary, he had a major coordinating role in realising the murder plan. He was ubiquitous, as the Trial Chamber found at judgement 1179, in particular in the Zvornik area during the mass executions from 14 to 16 July, as well as thereafter. The Chamber properly assessed his role as security branch officer, along with evidence clearly demonstrating that together with Beara, he obtained access to resources and personnel through the Drina Corps brigades in order to carry out the detention, execution and burial of thousands of prisoners. Your Honours, I now turn to your question. In section 5 of our response brief, at paragraphs 272 to 317, we have provided the response to all the Defence challenges regarding the Chamber's evaluation of the forensic and DNA evidence, including the challenges repeated here today. We rely on those responses -- on that response. Now, as one of his challenges to the number of victims, Popovic has argued that the Trial Chamber erred in convicting him for the execution of more than 1.000 males at Kozluk on 15 July, while the indictment only charged him with killing about 500 Muslim men at that location. It's at Popovic appeal brief paragraphs 438, 442 to 443, as well as reply at para 132. The first part of your question, Your Honours, invites the parties to discuss the Trial Chamber's interpretation of paragraphs 30.8.1 and 30.10 of the indictment at footnote 1839 of the trial judgement; and second, we are invited to discuss whether Popovic was convicted for any killings in excess of those pleaded in these two provisions. Your Honours, the short answer to both parts of your question is that the indictment provided Popovic with notice that there were approximately 1.000 victims at Kozluk. Popovic was therefore not convicted for killings in excess of those pleaded. To provide a bit more detail to the first part of your question, Your Honours, the Trial Chamber at footnote 1839 noted as follows: "The indictment alleges that approximately 500 Bosnian Muslim males were detained in the Rocevic school and then transported to a site near Kozluk and executed. Indictment paras 30.8.1 and 30.10. The Trial Chamber notes that the victims detained at Rocevic school are the same killed near Kozluk." Your Honours, based on a plain reading of the indictment, the two paragraphs referred to by the Trial Chamber in this footnote are cumulative. They are not overlapping. Specifically, paragraph 30.8.1 alleges that approximately 500 Rocevic prisoners were taken to Kozluk and executed, while paragraph 30.10 alleges that about 500 other Srebrenica-related prisoners captured from the column or separated at Potocari were executed at Kozluk. Read together, these two paragraphs put Popovic on notice that there were approximately 1.000 victims at Kozluk. The Prosecution pre-trial brief, at paragraphs 83 to 87, also did the same. In any event, Your Honours, even though the trial footnote -- Trial Chamber footnote might be a little ambiguous, it is clear that the Trial Chamber understood what the Prosecution was charging because at paragraph 794(11), it found that: "On 15 July, over 1.000 Bosnian Muslims were killed at Kozluk." It did so referring to paragraphs 517 to 524, and it based its conclusion upon eyewitness and forensic evidence available at trial. As a result, to answer your second question, Your Honours, Popovic was not convicted for any killings in excess of those pleaded in these two provisions. In any event, Your Honours, the indictment has at all times provided Popovic with fair notice of the large scale of allegations that he faced. Since the earliest form of the indictment against Popovic, he has been on notice that he was charged for his participation in the joint criminal enterprise to murder which resulted in the summary execution of over 7.000 Bosnian Muslim men and boys from Srebrenica. This is at indictment paragraphs 25, 27 to 29, and 37. At no point in the Prosecution's case did this total figure of alleged victims change. This concludes my submissions, Your Honours. Unless you have any questions, my colleague Ms. Najwa Nabti will conclude our response to Popovic's appeal challenges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. NABTI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Najwa Nabti, and I will address Popovic's arguments regarding his conviction for genocide. Popovic has challenged the Trial Chamber's finding that he had genocidal intent, as well as its general finding that a genocide was committed. I will address his arguments in turn, starting with his own genocidal intent. As you have just heard, Popovic knew about and participated vigorously in almost every step of the murder operation, from the formulation of the plan to the large-scale killings and burials. At Orahovac, Rocevic school and Pilica alone, Popovic participated in the killing of thousands of Bosnian Muslims, securing executioners, fuel, vehicles, whatever was needed to get the job done. Popovic's own words, the systematic exclusive targeting of Bosnian Muslims, and his destructive and discriminatory acts against them provided further evidence revealing his state of mind. These findings are at the trial judgement paragraphs 178 to 180. On this evidence, the Chamber was fully justified in finding that Popovic intended to destroy the Muslim population of Eastern Bosnia. Given the strength of the Trial Chamber's conclusion, it is no surprise that Popovic challenges the underlying findings throughout his brief. My colleagues have already addressed the reasonableness of those findings and they are fully canvassed in our brief. Popovic does not challenge the Trial Chamber's reliance on such factors as the scale of the atrocities, or the intent to commit the underlying acts, to infer genocidal intent, nor could he, as appellate jurisprudence clearly supports the Trial Chamber's approach. See the trial judgement paragraph 823 with citations to Jelisic, Blagojevic and Jokic, and the Krstic appeal judgements. The Trial Chamber's conclusion on Popovic's genocidal intent is well-founded and should be affirmed. In addition to its finding on Popovic's liability for genocide, the Chamber found that a genocide occurred. Popovic's challenges to this finding primarily pertain to the inference that the mass killings were perpetrated with genocidal intent. Since Popovic was convicted of committing genocide as a JCE member, proving the genocidal intent of the physical perpetrators of the underlying acts was not required, and so this finding was not a necessary pillar to his conviction as he suggests. This has been recently confirmed by the Appeals Chamber in its Rule 98 bis judgement in Karadzic at paragraph 79. Nonetheless, the Trial Chamber's findings that there was a -- that a genocide was -- had occurred were eminently reasonable. The Trial Chamber found that, in a matter of days, members of the Bosnian Serb forces systematically rounded up, detained, transported, executed, and buried thousands of Muslim men and boys. As the Defence points out, the Trial Chamber relied on significant coordination and the vast process entailed by this operation, but this only formed part of the Trial Chamber's analysis, which appears at paragraphs 856 to 863, leading to its conclusion that: "The scale and nature of the murder operation, the targeting of the victims, the systematic and organised manner in which it was carried out, and the plain intention to eliminate every Bosnian Muslim male who was captured or surrendered proves beyond reasonable doubt that members of the Bosnian Serb forces, including members of the VRS ... and security branch, intended to destroy the Muslims of Eastern Bosnia as a group." In addition, the Trial Chamber drew further support for genocidal intent from other culpable acts systematically directed against the same group, in particular the frenzied efforts to forcibly remove the remainder of the population while the male members of the community were targeted for murder. That's at paragraph 862. Popovic's claim that the Chamber found that all members of the Bosnian Serb forces committed genocide is unjustified, as it clearly mischaracterises the Trial Chamber's conclusion that genocide was committed by "members of the Bosnian Serb forces, including members of the VRS Main Staff and the VRS security branch, such as Popovic and Beara ..." That's at trial judgement paragraph 863. Popovic also faults the Trial Chamber for declining to specify which of these members committed genocide. However, the Appeals Chamber in Krstic confirmed that the inference of genocidal intent for a particular atrocity may be -- can be made without attributing that intent to specified individuals. That's at the Krstic appeal judgement paragraphs 34 and 35. In addition, the Defence answers its own complaint that some others who were involved in the killing, who are not on trial here, have not been convicted of genocide, by pointing out "that the genocidal intent of the perpetrator must be established only on a case-by-case basis." That's transcript of today's hearing at page 27. The Trial Chamber did so in this case, with respect to the convictions entered for genocide. With regard to Popovic's remaining challenges, the Trial Chamber has considered and rejected these arguments and its approach is consistent with appellate case law. Specifically, Popovic argues that for genocidal intent to be inferred, all Bosnian Muslims in Srebrenica would have to be targeted. He claims that the women, children, the elderly, and the members of the 28th ABiH column, which broke -- division column which broke through to ABiH-held territory were spared. First, the law is clear that killing all members of the group is not required to prove genocidal intent, as "the intent to destroy formed by a perpetrator of genocide will always be limited by the opportunity presented to him." That's in the Krstic appeal judgement at paragraph 13. Second, Popovic's arguments ignore the facts. The Chamber found that not even a cursory attempt was made to distinguish between civilian and soldier in separating the Bosnian Muslim males targeted for execution. Some children and elderly persons were among those executed. Indeed, the Trial Chamber heard evidence about the killing of a boy who pleaded for his life. They surely were not spared. Those findings are in the trial judgement at paragraphs 519, 779, 860, 866, and 990. And as noted, the frenzied efforts to forcibly remove the remaining population, described today by counsel as the transport of 20 to 30.000 Muslims to safety, provided further support for genocidal intent as other culpable acts systematically directed against the same group. That's at trial judgement paragraph 862. The Trial Chamber's approach is consistent with the Appeals Chamber's assessments on this issue in Krstic at paragraphs 31 to 33, and Blagojevic and Jokic at paragraph 123. The Trial Chamber also considered and rejected Popovic's argument that executing the thousands of Bosnian Muslim males was in response to any serious military threat they posed. Those targeted had already surrendered. Whether or not the column itself was a legitimate military target has nothing to do with the slaughter of the thousands of men and boys in custody. Popovic also misrepresents the fate of the ABiH 28th Division column by suggesting that there was no intent to destroy the men in the column who were ultimately allowed to pass. There is no question that Bosnian Serb forces would have killed these men if they were able to. Bosnian Serb forces attacked the column on 12 and 13 July and induced thousands to surrender, only to execute them shortly afterwards. Trial judgement paragraphs 380 to 383. The surviving members of the column were only allowed through when it was determined that blocking them was not feasible. Trial judgement paragraphs 551 to 560. Bosnian Serb forces then scoured the terrain to find those who did not make it through, ensuring "that no Bosnian Muslim male escaped the grasp of the VRS Main Staff and security branch." That's at trial judgement paragraph 860. The perpetrators of the genocide fully seized the opportunity presented to them after the fall of Srebrenica, killing as many as they could as quickly as they could. And again, Popovic gets no help from appellate jurisprudence which clearly supports the Trial Chamber's approach, in the Krstic appeal judgement at paragraphs 26 and 27. Finally, Popovic 's arguments ignore the Chamber's findings that Bosnian Serb forces perpetrated genocidal acts against the survivors who suffered profound physical and psychological harm as a result of the murder operation. In paragraph 30 of his reply brief, Popovic suggests that there was insufficient evidence of the physical and psychological harm to the surviving family members which he equates with "the harm of everyone who has lost his family member or friend under any circumstance." His claim that "the mental harm suffered by the relatives of the deceased is a natural part of everyday life" is not only repugnant but is contradicted by the evidence in this case. The extreme emotional and psychological distress caused by the taking and killing of thousands of fathers, sons, husbands, and brothers was evident not only from the Rule 92 bis statements of surviving family members but also from the testimony of witnesses to the suffering, expert evidence, and judicially noticed adjudicated facts. For example, Rahima Malkic, who fled her village near Srebrenica, recalled the moment when Serb soldiers took her husband away in Potocari. He looked at his family and said this was his fate. She also lost two sons but can't bear the thought of going to identify their bodies. She said: "I don't want to go back to my village. I can't take going back through Kravica because that's where my son was killed ... it's hard for me when I see young boys going to school ... I see the pictures of the fall of Srebrenica in my mind ... the pictures of my children come to me." That's at Exhibit P3229. Equally devastating is the evidence of PW-121, whose 14-year-old son was forcibly taken from her at Potocari, which can be found in Exhibit P2226, with further information about her child's tragic fate referenced in the Prosecution's closing arguments at T 34208 to 34210. The suffering inflicted on Rahima Malkic and PW-121 cannot possibly be characterised as mental harm suffered "as a natural part of everyday life." Rather, their evidence clearly shows that they suffer a grave and long-term disadvantage to their ability to lead a normal and constructive life. And yet, it is not unique. Thousands of Bosnian Muslims have suffered such a loss as a result of the mass killings, as described in the trial judgement at paragraphs 846 and 847. Others who have borne witness to their suffering came to testify. UN Military Observer Colonel Kingori described the tearful and terrifying separation process at Potocari, when men and boys were forcibly taken from their families. That's at transcript pages 19251 to 19257. UNPROFOR Civil Affairs Officer Edward Joseph testified that the overwhelming source of distress for the refugees who arrived in Tuzla around 12 or 13 July 1995 "was their concern about the fate of their men, be they husbands, fathers, sons or brothers, whom they had left behind." Transcript pages 14151 to 14152. The serious physical and mental harm inflicted as a result of the killings is further supported by expert evidence in Exhibit P2228 and by adjudicated facts 505 to 513. On all the evidence, Your Honours, Popovic was rightly convicted of committing genocide against the Muslims of Eastern Bosnia by killing members of the group and inflicting serious bodily and mental harm on the victims, their families and survivors. He was at the heart of the operation that accomplished the violent eradication of thousands of Bosnian Muslim men and boys in only a few days' time, and inflicted emotional and physical scars on the surviving population that will persist for generations. Your Honours should affirm his conviction and life sentence. Unless Your Honours have any questions, that concludes the Prosecution's submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I thank you very much. It appears to be convenient for us to take the break now, and resume at -- we will take the break for 25 minutes, a Solomonic decision. --- Break taken at 4.10 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, counsel, for the reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. A complex matrix of findings as mentioned by the Prosecution does not immunise the judgement from assessment on appeal. Contrary to the Prosecution assertion, these key evidentiary and factual findings highlighted in the appeal when undermined no longer sustain Popovic's conviction. The Defence submits that the standards in the jurisprudence relied on by the Prosecution in the beginning of its submissions wholly apply to this situation. Indeed, it is the Defence submission that it is dubious and the Trial Chamber managed to find Momir Nikolic and PW-168, in particular, to be credible on the crucial matters of fact that led to Popovic's conviction for genocide and where no direct corroboration was offered. The executions described in that event are indeed tragic, but it is notable how even that handful of survivors or executioners at the killing sites were entirely unable to identify Popovic as present. The Defence would encourage Your Honours not to abide by the Prosecution's efforts to affect your emotions in lieu of your reason in making your decision. The Prosecution's assertion that all the evidence was carefully reviewed is not apparent in respect of the challenged portion of the judgement indicated today and in the brief where it was argued that the Chamber had completely disregarded the evidence. This is especially true where Popovic has argued that no mention of major discrepancies were made, or where they were unfairly diminished to the prejudice of the accused despite the major contradictions of the evidence. For example, the appeal brief, paragraph 301, judgement footnote 1772. There is a serious danger where findings on the totality of mutual reinforcing pieces of evidence, as stated by the Prosecution at page 79 today, are molded with a goal of securing conviction rather than justice. The Prosecution's citation to the trial judgement at length presumes the impugned judgement's legitimacy as though it were an infallible record of fact. Indeed, the Prosecution can cite only indirect or circumstantial evidence to corroborate the most extensively challenged findings of fact in the appeal, ones that link Popovic directly to responsibility or command at execution sites. As explained in the appeal brief, the Trial Chamber applied obvious double-standards to witnesses depending on the incriminating value of their account. This is particularly true in respect of Kosoric, who provided substantially different evidence and who, as a witness, was severely disadvantaged in comparison to Momir Nikolic. The Trial Chamber therefore failed to apply the in dubio pro reo standard to prejudice of Mr. Popovic. Momir Nikolic was found by the Chamber to be only partially credible. It is worth repeating that this credibility assessment was selective. Only the most incriminating accounts were believed, whereas other accounts were not accepted without corroboration. In this way, the Chamber deviated from its own standard for its assessment of witnesses noted at paragraph 53 of the judgement. Reliability of the statement is not bolstered by Momir Nikolic's self-incrimination relating to the Hotel Fontana meeting. Specifically, Momir Nikolic's plea agreement was only accepted upon his addition of this account to his testimony, implying that he had a strong incentive to incriminate himself further. The Defence also submits that the Trial Chamber erred in relying on post hoc evidence to support major factual findings. It could be seen in appeal brief paragraphs 125, 126, and 316, and 319. This was by definition unreasonable. In respect of Your Honours' question, the Prosecution misrepresents the notice of the cause of killings. I will quote footnote 1839 for Your Honours: "The indictment alleges that approximately 500 Bosnian Muslim males were detained in Rocevic school and then transported to a site near Kozluk and executed." It is in the indictment paragraphs 30.8.1 and 30.10. "The Trial Chamber notes that the victims detained at Rocevic school are the same killed near Kozluk." The Prosecution argued that Popovic erroneously cited only one paragraph of the indictment as relevant to the Kozluk executions, ignored the related allegations concerning the Rocevic school, where approximately 500 Bosnian Muslim males were detained before being executed on the bank of the Drina River near Kozluk on 14 and 15 July, and that provided sufficient notice. On the contrary, the Trial Chamber explicitly noted that the victims detained at Rocevic school were the same killed near Kozluk. The indictment charged that 500 men, footnote 1839, fails to explain its decision to double the murder number of victims. It is a dangerous and indeed irresponsible precedent to flagrantly - or as the Prosecution conceded at paragraph 83 a little ambiguously - double the number of killings charged or to suggest the death of 500 more people is somehow immaterial or not requiring notice. At transcript page 80, the Prosecution repeats a major translation error that was addressed at length in his brief. Pandurevic was not told that Popovic would arrive to "sort the matter out." As noted in Popovic brief at paragraphs 361 through 364, he would come to say "what should be done." Not to sort the matter out. There are far more serious implications in the latter than the former. The Prosecution's argument that the Bosnian Serb forces had genocidal intent possesses a dangerous precedent as well to encourage the Appeal Chamber and condone the Trial Chamber's decision to impute genocidal intent onto an entire group of people who have not been identified and who have had no opportunity to confront the evidence or witnesses which allege this. In response to other assertions made by the Prosecution today, Popovic stands by his submissions in his appeal and reply and they need not be repeated here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We are going to continue the proceedings, moving now to the appeal of Mr. Beara, and we'll hear from counsel for Mr. Beara. Mr. Ostojic, we will stop at 5.15.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May it please the Court. Your Honours, again, my name is John Ostojic. On behalf of Mr. Beara, I'm here with my colleague Norman Sepenuk, and we will be providing the oral submissions to our appellate brief and to try to establish for this Chamber where we believe the Trial Court made several rather significant errors, both legally and in the factual basis of some of the evidence. I'm going to just initially in my opening remarks perhaps give you a road map as to where I think our submissions will lead. Initially, we were going to start with Mr. Sepenuk addressing from a strictly legal standpoint the issue of genocide. The issue of genocide and how it relates to Mr. Beara and how it was an erroneous decision by the Court as a matter of law. Following that submission, I will address this Chamber and particularly one item, the JCE 1, to commit murder. I think when this Chamber -- as our submission will reveal, the Trial Court relied on specifically one piece of evidence that we believe should not have been relied upon and most definitely there should have been no weight given to that evidence, specifically the testimony, as I'm sure you've read from the trial record is -- and from our briefs, is the testimony of a person called Miroslav Deronjic. He was submitted as a witness pursuant to 92 quater and we've objected at that time to his evidence being submitted because it goes strictly and specifically to the acts and conduct of Mr. Beara. The Trial Chamber at that time erred, although I'm going to highlight for you are their opinion, when they state that they will with extreme caution or at least with caution examine his testimony and make sure that there is corroborating evidence as to any acts or conversations that Mr. Deronjic would relay to this Chamber. They failed to do that. They not only failed to keep their promise, they, in fact, did the opposite. They relied solely on Mr. Deronjic's testimony in order to convict Mr. Beara. They relied solely on Mr. Deronjic's testimony to find him as a participant in the JCE 1 to commit murder. We believe that the trial record, as my learned colleague Mr. Rogers said, should be examined on the four squares that it is presented to you and not through extraneous or misleading or speculative reasoning. The Trial Chamber did just that. They went beyond the four squares to reach conclusions, to reach conclusions that were adverse to Mr. Beara and we believe that it was the convictions that led to Mr. Beara were erroneous by the Trial Chamber. I will in detail address Mr. Deronjic tomorrow on the acts and the conversations that the Trial Chamber relied upon, and I'm just giving you a brief overview. Next we are going to talk about the whereabouts of Mr. Beara. I think, with all due respect to the Trial Chamber, they misunderstood and certainly misapplied the Defence position with respect to the whereabouts of Mr. Beara. We contend and we've established through what we believe was credible evidence of where Mr. Beara was at certain critical times. We will examine for this Chamber not all the witnesses, so we will not go through each witness painstakingly, but we will highlight one witness and that witness that we will highlight for the benefit of my learned colleagues is Mr. Egbers. Mr. Egbers was a UN DutchBat officer. He was one witness who claims that he saw Mr. Beara at Nova Kasaba on July -- I believe it was the 13th or 14th of 1995. Who has the burden of proof in this case? According to the Trial Chamber, the Defence does. There was no corroboration of Mr. Egbers' testimony other than his self-corroborating statements or records. There was no extrinsic evidence to find that Mr. Beara was at Nova Kasaba. The Prosecution was required under the law of this jurisprudence to bring in corroborating evidence. Did they? Before we answer that question, I think perhaps it's more important to note, could they have? Could the Prosecution have brought in corroborating evidence if they believed it? They know the answer is yes, for a number of reasons. One, their own 65 ter witness on their list was a gentleman by the name of Zoran Malinic. Zoran Malinic purportedly was at this meeting with --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: I don't think it's appropriate to be referring to evidence outside of the record if it is not in the record as to what it may have been because it invites the speculation that criticism is being made of the Trial Chamber and is now inviting to you speculate on what it might have been. It's not proper. If my learned friend thinks that there is additional evidence that could be brought by 115, he should have done it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No. In fact, that's incorrect and I respectfully disagree. The evidence by Mr. Egbers identifies Zoran Malinic being at the meeting. The Prosecution argued in their opening statement, which is part of the record, and in their brief which they cite also both pre-trial and in other manners that Zoran Malinic was present. But, yes, their fallback argument is that he's probably a Serb, which he was, a member of the VRS --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before you proceed, you had earlier said, according to the Trial Chamber, the Defence has the burden of proof. Do you mean by that that the Trial Chamber explicitly said that or do you mean that that is something that can be fairly deduced from the record?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. By no means would I ever suggest that they expressly stated that. It's clearly implicit when they took the evidence of Mr. Egbers and failed to understand why and who had the burden of proof to corroborate that evidence. So indeed it was not expressly stated by the Trial Chamber, but we believe just looking at that evidence which we'll share tomorrow that, in fact, they did shift the burden of proof. And instead of suggesting that the Prosecution bring corroborating evidence, they simply relied on that evidence and dismissed the Defence evidence on that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Speaking personally, I would prefer if you, rather than give the overview, give us your submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, it's quite lengthy but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Because I don't want to you spend the time giving us an overview, the remaining time, we want to hear your submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, this is part of my submission. Within the submission I did have this part of the overview, so I am highlighting it and then we are going to go into detail on it but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, it's your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The Prosecution not only had the opportunity and the burden of proof to call --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SEKULE
utterances.text: I just wanted to understand so that I can follow on my part. Your learned colleague said that that wasn't -- the issue that you addressed previously was not in evidence and you make -- you did give a response to that. I want to know that kind -- that response, is it your submission that that evidence that you referred to is actually into evidence? I just want to understand that aspect. Arising from what was your learned colleague's submissions. If you may clarify, I just simply want to understand exactly what is the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. To clarify, is it evidence, I suggest that it is and it's found in the testimony of Mr. Egbers, number 1. It's part of the trial record below as the briefs are, as counsel cited to his initial pre-trial brief. That evidence is at least those two instances. It's also present in our request to try to bring the witness but I don't believe that was marked as evidence. But I believe that in at least those two separate occasions, that evidence was presented to the Trial Chamber. And also, if recollection serves me well, I believe it was also addressed in their opening statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Counsel, can you please give us, for our -- the references in the trial record as to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will be able to do that tomorrow morning, and I apologise for that. I don't want to give you the wrong cite. I will prepare that and make sure you have that first thing in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So as I've stated, we will talk about how the Trial Chamber erred as a matter of law and as a matter of fact, both as to Mr. Deronjic, and highlight the second part as a matter of fact with respect to Mr. Egbers and the evidence about Mr. Beara's whereabouts. Next, we will talk about or we expect to discuss with this Chamber another witness, a gentleman by the name -- or another person by the name of Milos Tomovic, and that goes to whereabouts also. The Trial Chamber misunderstood the argument that we had with Milos Tomovic. He was a witness that the Prosecution was expecting to call. It was a witness the Prosecution actually took, I think, twice met with him and got his statement, and ultimately it was a witness that the Prosecution interviewed without the assistance of counsel, without him being sworn, it was at that, and we tried to submit that to the Trial Chamber, and part of that evidence was in -- specifically introduced through the cross-examination of Mr. Pandurevic. In those questionings by the Prosecution, they expressly asked Mr. Tomovic, by prefacing the question, "We know at that time," namely, the 13th through the 15th, "that Beara was in Belgrade." The Trial Chamber failed to recognise the importance and significance of that. Who was Milos Tomovic? And why is he important? He was Mr. Beara's driver. He was a critical witness that could substantiate or verify either the Prosecution's case or the Defence case. Was it our burden of proof or the Prosecution's? They chose not to call him. We'll further discuss portions of our Defence case that I believe the Trial Chamber erroneously summarily dismissed without giving a reasoned opinion. The Trial Chamber's conclusions with respect to the Defence case did not meet the requirements of a reasoned opinion. Compounding this lack of reasoning are the Trial Chamber's inconsistent and contradictory findings as they relate to Mr. Beara. Ultimately, and early on we will address the question that the Court raised with us, specifically the necessary link with respect to Jadar River and the Trnovo killings. Our next piece or portion of our argument is going to relate to seeking the truth that the Tribunal and all of us have an opportunity to try to the best of our abilities to get to the truth. We will highlight several pieces of evidence that have been introduced in this case, specifically when we talk about the victims, when we talk about the numbers on this case, not to be cold, not to be dismissive of the terrible things that occurred to those people and those families, a UN officer, Mr. Egbers, and I think my learned colleague mentioned him -- I'm sorry, not Mr. Egbers, Mr. Ed Joseph, excuse me. He mentions in his report early on that his observation was that 3.000 Bosnian Muslim men were killed in legitimate combat engagements, mines, and during other activities. The Trial Chamber simply ignores that, dismisses that evidence as if it's non-existent. It was not a report created or generated by a Bosnian Serb. It was indeed from a third party, a UN staff officer. So when we are seeking the truth, we should examine all the evidence and try to determine was it 2.000, 5.000 or 7.000 that unfortunately suffered the fate in July of 1995. Other what I consider to be items that the Court simply ignored: When the Court balanced Mr. Beara's purported words, it cautiously, methodically stated that Mr. Beara was using code, didn't want people to know. When we presented the evidence of Mr. Vasic, Dragomir Vasic, who was the head of the MUP, the police, in his report he essentially says the VRS are no longer in charge of these prisoners and essentially he claims that he's going to liquidate 5.000 of them. In the evidence of Mr. Butler, his response when confronted on cross-examination as to who bore the responsibility to detain and who ultimately stated expressly directly that they were going to liquidate and kill those people, Mr. Butler claims he didn't mean it, as if he knew. The Trial Chamber ignored that evidence which points directly in a different direction than it does to Mr. Beara. We'll also talk about what I've coined exculpatory evidence. There is two things. We have mentioned one with Milos Tomovic, Mr. Beara's driver, but the other significant piece of evidence that I think we should address is what we coined previously as the Croat intercept. Mr. Beara was being overheard in certain conversations. This one intercept in the middle of what was the worst crimes that had occurred since World War II, Mr. Beara does not discuss killings, in code or otherwise. He clearly says: Move the men to Batkovici camp, which was a known, recognised detention centre, not to Pilica, not to some other area or other school, but to the detention centre where everyone expected them to go. The Trial Chamber surprisingly, without any reasoning behind it, simply stated this was code again. Mr. Beara knew he was being listened to. Mr. Beara knew that someone was going to overhear him so he misled everyone by giving this Croat intercept. If that's true, and we accept that logic, how then can they claim the other intercepts point towards Mr. Beara for either being a participant in the JCE 1 or having any genocidal intent? Finally, with your permission, we will address sentencing. The two aspects of it we believe that the Court, the Trial Chamber, legally erred or erred as a matter of law, I should say, excuse me, when it failed to apply the law once it recognised that there existed mitigating circumstances. It recognised three, but at the end of the day it gave Mr. Beara the harshest sentence available. Likewise, the Trial Chamber erred in fact because they didn't give sufficient weight to those mitigating circumstances, giving only limited or what they called nominal weight to those mitigating circumstances. Finally, we will address the aggravating factor where the Court we believe failed as a matter of law and only -- erred as a matter of law and only utilised the same underlying facts that they convicted him to suggest that they were an aggravation and thereby sentenced him too harshly. The Trial Chamber has indeed applied the wrong legal standard in assessing Ljubisa Beara's contribution to the JCE. I believe that it might be a good time to stop, with your permission, so that we don't overlap. And I'll tomorrow present specific details and address the questions that were raised today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, before you rise, may I just make one small point relating to my concern about Mr. Malinic. So that it's clear what my concern is because it may arise tomorrow if there is reference to other witnesses that did not testify. My concern is not that there may have been mentioned to Zoran Malinic as being someone who may have been present but more to what he might have been able to say, which is speculative. Obviously if there had been interviews or it was known to the Defence that there were interviews relating to the individual, that's one thing, but it's not appropriate to refer, and I don't know whether my learned friend was going to, to refer to anything that that witness may have said because that is not in the record. And that was my concern, and just so we are all clear about what the nature of my concern is, I hope that's now clear. There shouldn't be reference, speculative reference about what witnesses who did not testify might have said. That's inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I could respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I appreciate my learned colleague trying to assist us in this manner, but I think he either misunderstood me or perhaps I wasn't eloquent in the rush to try to get it done. We are not going to suggest what Mr. Malinic said. We are suggesting that if there is evidence with respect to the whereabouts of Mr. Beara, there should be some corroboration of each of those witnesses and I know that they would rather have a quantity, and they talk about quantity more than quality, but I suggest to this Chamber that you should look at each witness and determine from that each witness whether there was corroborating evidence. With respect to Mr. Egbers, the Prosecution had the burden of proof, they had the opportunity, they interviewed him, they know what he said, they identified him, they did not bring him in court. The inference that I can draw is that he would have been adverse to them and that's accurate. The inference the Trial Chamber should have drawn was that he was going to be inconsistent and would not corroborate his testimony, but I do appreciate my learned friend's guidance on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let us wait until tomorrow to see what is your precise submission, and what, if any, is the precise response from opposing counsel, though I should encourage the parties to allow the appeal to proceed as quickly as possible and with the least interruption. I'm not accustomed to appeals being conducted in a manner where there are objections. It looks more like a trial. That I'm accustomed to. So let us try to proceed as smoothly and as quickly as possible tomorrow, with as little interruption as possible. Thank you. We are adjourned.
